stories.title: Bortoleto shuts down Audi exit talk with a 'no clauses' contract
stories.what_happened: Bortoleto told media this week he has a **long-term, multi-year contract** with Audi that runs well beyond 2026. Asked about its structure, he said **"there are no clauses"** — notable in a sport where driver deals are usually loaded with performance triggers and team options. He confirmed he'll be at Audi **"next year, and not only next year, but for the following years as well,"** with reports suggesting the deal stretches toward Audi's 2030 target. The statement directly addresses swirling rumors that Audi could pursue Sainz or Piastri for 2027. It lands as Audi endures a difficult first season as a full works team, sitting near the back of the constructors' standings.
key_points: Bortoleto says his Audi deal has **no exit clauses**, unusual for F1 contracts
Deal runs **beyond 2026**, toward Audi's stated **2030** project target
He's scored **10 of Audi's 12 points** in 2026, the team's top scorer
Move addresses rumors linking **Carlos Sainz** and **Oscar Piastri** to his seat
Audi is in its **debut season** as a full manufacturer works team

depth.background: Audi entered Formula 1 in 2026 as a full works manufacturer, absorbing the former **Sauber** team, with boss **Mattia Binotto** framing it as a long-term project aimed at real competitiveness by **2030**. **Gabriel Bortoleto**, a 21-year-old Brazilian, joined as a rookie in 2025 (Sauber's final season) and has been the team's most productive scorer through a rocky debut works season. Speculation had linked bigger names — Sainz and even reigning-form McLaren driver Piastri — to a future Audi seat, raising doubts about Bortoleto's own long-term status at the team.

stories.title: Verstappen's Red Bull exit clause is live — and the contract offers keep shifting
stories.what_happened: Verstappen went into F1's summer break sitting sixth in the championship, more than **100 points** off leader Kimi Antonelli, which mathematically triggered the exit clause in his contract. That set off weeks of contract theater: Red Bull first proposed a short, one-year extension to 2029 that would strip the exit clause out of his deal in exchange for more money, then reportedly pivoted to offering a much longer **five-year contract taking him to 2033**. Neither offer has been publicly accepted. When a report circulated suggesting Max was already leaning toward re-signing without the clause, his father and manager Jos Verstappen bluntly dismissed it online. Team boss-level sources say Red Bull is trying to lock him down before rival teams can make a serious approach during the clause window, which stays open until October.
key_points: Verstappen sits **P6** in the drivers' championship with **109 points**, well outside the top two he needed to stay above to keep his contract locked in — so his exit clause is now officially active
He has until **October 2026** to decide whether to use that clause and leave Red Bull for 2027
Red Bull first offered a **one-year extension to 2029** that would delete the exit clause entirely, then reportedly switched to a **five-year deal running to 2033**
His father and manager **Jos Verstappen** publicly shot down reports of a done deal, replying "You know absolutely nothing" to a report claiming Max was close to re-signing
Red Bull remains the only front-running team yet to win a race in **2026**, fueling speculation about why Verstappen hasn't jumped at a new deal

depth.background: Max Verstappen, a **four-time world champion**, is contracted to Red Bull through the end of **2028**, but that deal contains a performance-linked exit clause: if he isn't in the top two of the standings by the summer break, he can trigger a route out for 2027. New engine and aerodynamic rules introduced this year have shaken up the competitive order, and Red Bull's 2026 car (the RB22) has been difficult to set up, leaving Verstappen well off the pace he's used to. He has openly criticized the new regulations this season.

stories.title: Government cuts export tax on petrol, diesel and jet fuel as crude prices ease
stories.what_happened: Effective **August 15, 2026**, India's government cut export duties on petrol, diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF). The **petrol export duty was scrapped entirely**, dropping from ₹3.5 per litre (set August 3) to **zero**. The **diesel** windfall tax was cut to **₹24/litre** from ₹25.5, and the **ATF** rate was cut to **₹19.5/litre** from ₹22. The finance ministry clarified there is **no change to domestic retail fuel prices** — these levies apply only to fuel Indian refiners sell abroad, not what consumers pay at the pump.
key_points: Export duty on **petrol cut to zero**, from **₹3.5/litre** charged just two weeks earlier.
**Diesel** export tax (SAED) cut to **₹24/litre**, down from **₹25.5**.
**ATF (jet fuel)** export tax cut to **₹19.5/litre**, down from **₹22**.
Domestic pump prices for petrol and diesel are **unchanged** — this only affects fuel sold abroad.

depth.background: India taxes fuel exports through a **'windfall tax'** (formally the Special Additional Excise Duty, SAED), first introduced in 2022 when refiners were earning outsized profits exporting fuel refined from cheap Russian crude while domestic supply tightened. The government reviews and adjusts these rates roughly every two weeks based on international oil and fuel prices — raising them when refiner margins spike, cutting them when crude prices fall. Less than two weeks before this cut, the government had actually **raised** these same export levies, reflecting how quickly crude markets have been swinging amid the broader Iran-linked Middle East tensions.

stories.title: India win the toss and bat first in their historic 600th Test, but leave uncapped Auqib Nabi out of the XI at Galle
stories.what_happened: Play began on schedule at **Galle International Stadium**, with India winning the toss and opting to bat first on what looked, in Gill's own assessment, like a good batting surface. The announced XI answered yesterday's open question: **Auqib Nabi did not get his debut**. Instead, India fielded three specialist spinners — Ravindra Jadeja, **Kuldeep Yadav**, and uncapped spinner Manav Suthar — alongside pacers Mohammed Siraj and Prasidh Krishna, betting on spin-friendly Galle conditions over an extra seamer. The top order got off to a rocky start when **Yashasvi Jaiswal was run out** within the first hour, before KL Rahul and Devdutt Padikkal steadied the innings; India were past 70 runs for one wicket as the morning session progressed. This is officially India's 600th Test and their first match of the new World Test Championship cycle, played under Gill's captaincy on a day that also happens to be India's Independence Day.
key_points: India **won the toss and chose to bat first** in what is officially their **600th Test match**, only the third team ever to reach that number.
Uncapped pacer **Auqib Nabi was left out of the XI** despite his shock call-up, with India instead picking **three spinners** — Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar.
Opener **Yashasvi Jaiswal was run out** inside the first hour, an early setback for the new-look batting order.
The Test is India's **first fixture of the 2025–2027 World Test Championship cycle** and the first under new full-time captain **Shubman Gill**.
August 15 is **India's Independence Day**, adding symbolic weight to a match already billed as a milestone occasion.

depth.background: This is the same landmark Test previewed a day earlier: India entering their 600th match, a mark only England and Australia had reached before, at Galle's 50th-ever Test — a first for any Asian venue. Shubman Gill leads the side for the first time in a bilateral Test series since being installed as India's full-time red-ball captain, working alongside head coach **Gautam Gambhir**. Ahead of the game, India's pace attack had already lost **Jasprit Bumrah** to a knee injury, prompting the surprise squad inclusion of uncapped Jammu and Kashmir seamer Auqib Nabi — whose potential debut was the single biggest open question heading into the match.

thread.previously: Yesterday's story previewed India's 600th Test — a milestone only England and Australia had previously reached — with Shubman Gill captaining and uncapped seamer Auqib Nabi in the squad after Jasprit Bumrah was ruled out injured; the open question was whether Nabi would get a shock debut.
thread.changed: The match has now actually started: India won the toss and chose to bat, and the announced XI leaves Auqib Nabi out — India went in with Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar as spinners alongside Jadeja instead of handing Nabi his debut. Play is underway, with India past 70 for the loss of Yashasvi Jaiswal, who was run out early.

stories.title: Opposition pounces on Modi's Independence Day speech fumble and 'dimaagi Naxal' remark
stories.what_happened: During his address, Modi appeared to **fumble while citing statistics on India's bioeconomy growth** since 2014, a moment Congress and AAP leaders quickly clipped and shared on social media. Congress's **Pawan Khera** described Modi as **"an under-confident, nervous and shaky Prime Minister,"** and AAP chief **Arvind Kejriwal** offered similar criticism of the delivery. Separately, a remark using the phrase **"dimaagi Naxal"** — loosely, someone who is a "Naxal [left-wing extremist] in their thinking" — aimed at critics of the government drew accusations of inflammatory, divisive language on a day meant to unite the country. Congress also renewed substantive criticism, accusing the government of a **"dishonest pitch"** on **women's reservation in Parliament** and of reversing its earlier opposition to a **caste census** before announcing one itself. The **BJP defended** the speech, casting it as a genuine roadmap for **"Viksit Bharat"** by 2047.
key_points: Modi **stumbled while citing bioeconomy growth figures** during his 80th Independence Day address from the Red Fort.
Congress's **Pawan Khera** called him **"under-confident, nervous and shaky"**; AAP's **Arvind Kejriwal** echoed the criticism.
A **"dimaagi Naxal"** (roughly, "Naxal in the mind") remark aimed at government critics drew sharp opposition backlash.
Congress accused the government of a **"dishonest pitch"** on women's reservation and flip-flopping on the **caste census**.
The **BJP has defended** the speech as a roadmap for a **"Viksit Bharat" (developed India)**.

depth.background: Every August 15, India's Prime Minister addresses the nation from the ramparts of the **Red Fort** in Delhi — the most-watched political speech of the year, traditionally used to set the government's agenda. This year marked India's **80th year of independence**, and Modi used the speech to announce a slate of new initiatives under the banner **"Shakti Ki Saptadhara."** Opposition parties, led by **Congress** and the **Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)**, routinely contest the government's framing and record in the speech's aftermath, and this year's reaction has focused as much on how Modi delivered the speech as on what he said.

stories.title: Bumrah's shock Sri Lanka Test withdrawal sparks an internal BCCI blame game, reports say
stories.what_happened: Fresh reporting says the sudden nature of Bumrah's withdrawal wasn't a simple case of a player failing a late fitness test — it has instead triggered an **internal BCCI storm** over who knew what and when. According to the reports, the **CoE's sports science team had indicated to Agarkar and the selectors that Bumrah would be fit enough to travel** for the series, only for a subsequent, more thorough medical assessment to reveal his knee injury required a **longer recovery period** than first thought, forcing his withdrawal after all. That gap between the CoE's initial read and the final medical picture has reportedly left the chief selector's panel unhappy with how the CoE handled and communicated Bumrah's case. Compounding the issue, the report notes the **CoE has been without a full-time head of sports science** since Nitin Patel departed the role — a structural gap that may have contributed to the mixed signals. The BCCI is now said to be reviewing its **injury-management and communication protocols**. J&K's uncapped **Auqib Nabi**, who took 104 wickets across the last two Ranji Trophy seasons, remains in as Bumrah's replacement.
key_points: Reports say India's selectors were told **Jasprit Bumrah would be fit** for the Sri Lanka Tests, only for a **later medical assessment** to rule him out.
The apparent miscommunication is between the **BCCI Centre of Excellence's sports science team** and **chief selector Ajit Agarkar's** panel.
The **Centre of Excellence has had no full-time head of sports science** since Nitin Patel's departure.
The BCCI is now said to be **reviewing its injury-management and communication process**.
Uncapped **Jammu and Kashmir pacer Auqib Nabi**, who took **104 wickets** over two Ranji Trophy seasons, was Bumrah's shock replacement.

depth.background: **Jasprit Bumrah** is India's premier fast bowler, and his fitness has been a recurring storyline for over a year because of a history of back trouble carefully managed through a workload-management system centered on the **BCCI's Centre of Excellence (CoE)** in Bengaluru. It was reported yesterday that Bumrah, who picked up a **knee injury** fielding in a one-day international against England in Cardiff in July, had been **ruled out of the two-Test series against Sri Lanka**, with uncapped pacer **Auqib Nabi** getting a shock call-up in his place. India's chief selector, **Ajit Agarkar**, leads the panel responsible for naming the Test squad, working off fitness assessments the CoE provides.

thread.previously: Bumrah had been ruled out of the Sri Lanka Test series with a knee injury, and India gave uncapped Auqib Nabi a shock call-up as his replacement.
thread.changed: New reporting says the withdrawal has triggered an internal BCCI storm — selectors were reportedly told Bumrah would be fit, only for a later assessment to rule him out, exposing a communication gap with the Centre of Excellence that the BCCI is now said to be reviewing.

stories.title: Ex-F1 steward Johnny Herbert asks if Aston Martin's woeful 2026 is the 'first sign' of Adrian Newey's decline
stories.what_happened: Speaking as F1's 2026 season paused for its summer break, former driver and ex-FIA steward Johnny Herbert said Aston Martin's dismal form this year could be the first real sign that Adrian Newey's dominant run as a designer is ending. Herbert pointed to the scale of what Aston Martin assembled around Newey — a new factory, major investment, and full technical authority — and said it was hard to understand 'how things have gone so wrong,' arguing Newey 'hasn't been able to put together a crew that is able to put together a good car.' Between them, drivers Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll have scored just one point all season, a result worse than every team except brand-new entrant Cadillac. Herbert asked directly: 'Is this the demise of Adrian Newey? The first sign of him being on a downward spiral? It happens in sport even to the very best.'
key_points: Former F1 driver and steward **Johnny Herbert** questioned whether Aston Martin's struggles mark the **'first sign'** of design legend **Adrian Newey's** decline.
Aston Martin lured Newey from Red Bull in 2025, making him a **5% shareholder** and technical partner for the team's 2026 car.
Despite Newey's involvement, Aston Martin has had one of the **worst starts of the modern F1 era**, with Alonso and Stroll combining for just **one point**.
Only **Cadillac**, F1's brand-new team, has fared worse than Aston Martin so far this season.
Herbert asked: **'Is this the demise of Adrian Newey?'** — questioning whether even F1's most decorated designer can be undone by team-building failures.

depth.background: **Adrian Newey** is widely regarded as the most successful car designer in Formula 1 history, having built championship-winning cars for Williams, McLaren, and Red Bull across three decades. In 2025, Aston Martin — owned by billionaire Lawrence Stroll — convinced Newey to leave Red Bull, giving him a 5% ownership stake and naming him managing technical partner to lead the team's car for F1's new 2026 technical regulations, alongside a brand-new factory built specifically to support him. Expectations were high given Newey's track record and the scale of investment behind him.

stories.title: Wolff credits a Schumacher-and-Hamilton veteran engineer for turning Kimi Antonelli into F1's youngest-ever points leader
stories.what_happened: Mercedes team principal **Toto Wolff** publicly praised Bonnington for shaping Antonelli's rapid rise, describing him as **"the optimum combination of an engineer, nerdy when he needs to be nerdy and to look at the science and the data, but also super compassionate when the driver needs support"** — both a **"good mentor"** and a **"strong boss."** In his second F1 season, Antonelli has won **5 of 7 races** so far in 2026 and become the sport's **youngest-ever championship leader**, holding a **41-point** lead over Hamilton in the standings.
key_points: Antonelli has **5 wins from 7 races** and leads the championship by **41 points**
He's F1's **youngest-ever championship leader**
Race engineer **Pete 'Bono' Bonnington** — who engineered Michael Schumacher, then Lewis Hamilton for 12 seasons — now guides him
Wolff calls Bonnington 'nerdy' with data but a **'strong boss'** who mentors Antonelli

depth.background: A Formula 1 race engineer is the driver's closest technical partner — in constant radio contact, managing strategy, car setup and in-race decisions. **Pete Bonnington** built his reputation over a long Mercedes career: he was **Michael Schumacher's** race engineer during Schumacher's Mercedes comeback, then spent **12 seasons** as **Lewis Hamilton's** engineer. When Hamilton left for Ferrari and Mercedes promoted rookie **Kimi Antonelli** for 2025, Bonnington stayed on to guide the teenager instead.

stories.title: Cricket Australia's chief backs cutting back 'meaningless' bilateral ODIs — but warns of a revenue hit
stories.what_happened: Speaking in Darwin during Australia's Test against Bangladesh, Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg said he agrees that international matches 'need to matter and have context and jeopardy,' adding: 'Creating jeopardy and meaning into the games we play is important.' His comments echo remarks made earlier in the week by ICC chief executive Sanjog Gupta, who said the era of 'randomly scheduled' bilateral series 'has to come to an end,' while arguing the ODI format can survive if it's tied more closely to the ODI World Cup. Greenberg noted Gupta had made similar comments directly to Cricket Australia staff during a recent visit to Melbourne. But Greenberg also flagged a real concern: bilateral ODIs currently make up a significant share of Cricket Australia's broadcast-rights revenue, so stripping them out entirely would have a commercial cost. Greenberg is a member of the ICC working group currently finalizing the Future Tours Programme — the internationally agreed cricket schedule — for 2028-31, and the group is also sketching an early, rough version of the following 2032-35 cycle.
key_points: Cricket Australia CEO **Todd Greenberg** says international cricket needs more **'jeopardy and meaning'**, backing a rethink of routine bilateral ODI series.
His comments echo **ICC CEO Sanjog Gupta**, who says the era of 'randomly scheduled' bilateral series 'has to come to an end'.
Greenberg flagged a real tension: bilateral ODIs make up a **significant share of Cricket Australia's broadcast revenue**.
Greenberg sits on the **ICC working group** now finalizing the international schedule for **2028-31**, and sketching an early draft for 2032-35.

depth.background: One-Day Internationals (ODIs) — 50-overs-a-side matches — sit between Test cricket's prestige and T20's popularity and money, and have increasingly been criticized as filler content when played as routine bilateral series between two countries outside a World Cup. Administrators, including the ICC's own CEO, have been signaling a shift toward tying ODIs more tightly to context that matters, like World Cup qualification, rather than filling the calendar with series that carry little stake.

stories.title: OpenAI tells European ChatGPT users ads are coming to the Free and Go plans this month
stories.what_happened: On the morning of **August 15**, OpenAI's Irish entity — which handles European users under EU law — sent a notification to everyone on ChatGPT's Free and Go plans in the EEA and Switzerland. It said **advertising will begin appearing in ChatGPT later this month**. Unlike a typical targeted ad, the initial European ads will be selected only from the topic of the conversation someone is currently having, plus coarse location and device data — not from past chats or OpenAI's memory of the user. Paying subscribers on Pro, Enterprise, Business and Education tiers are explicitly excluded and will not see ads. OpenAI says a future personalised-ads option will require users to **opt in**, and it has updated its privacy policy to spell out how ad selection, measurement and controls work.
key_points: OpenAI Ireland emailed Free and Go plan users in the **EEA and Switzerland** at 08:29 today saying ads start **later this month**.
Ads will **not** be personalised at launch in Europe — targeting is limited to the **current chat topic, rough location, and device type**.
**Pro, Enterprise, Business and Education** subscribers stay ad-free; only the free tiers see ads.
OpenAI is updating its **privacy policy** to explain how the ads are chosen, measured, and controlled.
The move follows OpenAI's **US ad test launched in February 2026** — Europe is the next, more heavily-regulated market.

depth.background: OpenAI has been burning through billions of dollars a year running ChatGPT, and until now made almost all its money from **subscriptions** (Plus, Pro, Business) rather than advertising. Earlier this year it began quietly testing ads for US free-tier users, a first for a company that built its brand on being subscription-funded and "user-aligned" rather than ad-funded like Google or Meta. Europe's EEA and Switzerland fall under the **GDPR** privacy regime, which is why OpenAI is rolling ads out more cautiously there — with no personalisation at first and a formal privacy-policy update.

stories.title: Modi sets a target of 100 GW nuclear power by 2047, a more than tenfold jump from today
stories.what_happened: In his **13th consecutive Independence Day address** from the Red Fort, PM Modi announced India is aiming for **100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047** — the year the country marks a century of independence — as part of his 'Viksit Bharat' (developed India) roadmap. He said India would commission and operationalise **five new nuclear reactors over the next 6-7 years**, and declared the country had this year achieved mastery of **Fast Breeder Reactor technology**, which lets a reactor generate more nuclear fuel than it consumes — a step Modi called crucial to atomic fuel self-reliance. The target marks a jump of more than **11 times today's roughly 8.8 GW** of installed nuclear capacity, which currently supplies only about 3% of India's power. The push builds on the 2025 SHANTI Act, which for the first time allows private firms to build and license nuclear facilities, plus the dedicated Nuclear Energy Mission funding SMRs. Modi explicitly framed the goal as an 'energy security' imperative, language that echoed growing unease in New Delhi about oil-supply risk following weeks of tension around the Strait of Hormuz.
key_points: PM Modi set a target of **100 GW of nuclear power by 2047**, the year India turns **100 years independent**.
That's more than **tenfold India's current nuclear capacity** of roughly **8.8 GW**.
India plans to commission **five new nuclear reactors within the next 6-7 years**.
The **2025 SHANTI Act** lets **private companies** build and run nuclear plants for the first time.
Modi says India achieved 'mastery' of **Fast Breeder Reactor technology** this year, a step toward fuel self-reliance.

depth.background: India's nuclear power program has been a tightly closed **government monopoly** run by the state-owned Nuclear Power Corporation of India (NPCIL) for decades, and today contributes only about **3% of India's electricity** despite the country being the world's most populous and one of its fastest-growing power markets. Because India sits outside the mainstream global nuclear trade regime, it has historically had restricted access to imported uranium fuel and foreign reactor technology, which slowed expansion for years. In 2025, Parliament passed the **SHANTI Act**, opening the sector to private investment for the first time, alongside a new Nuclear Energy Mission that has earmarked **Rs 20,000 crore** for small modular reactors (SMRs). Modi's 100 GW target, unveiled from the Red Fort on India's **80th Independence Day**, is the most explicit numeric goal any government has put on the country's atomic-energy ambitions.

stories.title: Modi's 'dimaagi Naxal' line in his Independence Day speech triggers a fierce BJP-Congress row over who counts as a threat
stories.what_happened: Speaking from the Red Fort on his 80th Independence Day address — his 13th consecutive one, and his shortest in four years at around 75 minutes — Modi said India has succeeded in clearing armed Naxals from the forests, but warned that 'dimaagi Naxals are looking for opportunities to create violence, unrest... they want to drag society on the wrong path.' He went further, saying such people 'have their place in the power corridors... were in government committees as advisors' and that 'Maoist thinking impacted policies,' calling on society to 'identify these ideological Naxalites and isolate them.' Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh hit back, calling it 'a sure sign of desperation' and arguing Modi 'ends up doing whatever these so-called urban Naxals or dimaagi Naxals are demanding' — a jab at policy inconsistency. BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari responded by saying Rahul Gandhi's own 'mindset reflects that of a dimaagi Naxal ecosystem.' The exchange continued into a second day of statements from both sides.
key_points: In his 80th Independence Day speech, Modi said armed Naxals are largely gone from India's forests but **'dimaagi Naxals'** — people with a Maoist mindset — remain, including inside **government advisory committees**.
Congress's **Jairam Ramesh** called it 'a sure sign of desperation,' arguing Modi is recycling his older 'urban Naxal' label under a new name.
BJP spokesperson **Pradeep Bhandari** turned the phrase back on the opposition, saying Rahul Gandhi's 'mindset reflects' that of a 'dimaagi Naxal ecosystem'.
The term has **no formal legal definition**, unlike 'Naxal', which refers to a decades-long armed Maoist insurgency in central-eastern India.
The row escalated into a second day of statements from both parties, continuing into today.

depth.background: **Naxalism** is a left-wing Maoist insurgency that has run in parts of central and eastern India for decades, and the government has said in recent years it has largely cleared armed Naxals from the forests they once controlled. For years, Modi and BJP leaders have also used the term **'urban Naxal'** to describe activists, academics, and government critics they accuse of sympathizing with Maoist ideology without taking up arms. By coining 'dimaagi Naxal' (literally 'mental/intellectual Naxal') and explicitly placing such people inside government committees, Modi appears to widen that label from outside critics to insiders shaping policy.

stories.title: Modi says India's 'Iron Dome' — the Sudarshan Chakra air shield — is progressing rapidly, a year after he announced it
stories.what_happened: In his 80th Independence Day address from the Red Fort, Modi said work on the Sudarshan Chakra system was moving quickly, though he did not give a specific deployment timeline. He paired the update with broader defence statistics — India's domestic defence output near **₹1.78 lakh crore** for FY26 and exports of **₹38,424 crore** to almost 100 countries — and urged greater investment in drone and counter-drone systems, framing self-reliant defence manufacturing as central to his 'Viksit Bharat' (developed India) vision.
key_points: PM Modi said the indigenous **Sudarshan Chakra** air defence shield, which he first announced exactly a year ago on Independence Day 2025, is progressing **"rapidly."**
India's domestic defence production has grown to **₹1.78 lakh crore** (about **$21 billion**) in FY26, up from just ₹46,000 crore in 2014.
Defence **exports** have risen roughly **50-fold** to **₹38,424 crore**, now reaching close to **100 countries**.
Modi also called for greater investment in **drones and counter-drone technology** as India pushes for defence self-reliance.

depth.background: Modi announced the Sudarshan Chakra project on Independence Day 2025, describing it as an Israel-style **Iron Dome** to shield vital military and civilian sites from missile and drone attack. The push for indigenous defence manufacturing has accelerated in recent years as India seeks to cut its historic reliance on imported weapons, particularly from Russia, and to build an export-capable defence industry of its own. The announcement also lands against a backdrop of recent India-Pakistan military tension and DRDO's stated role in prior cross-border operations.

stories.title: Modi unveils 'Shakti Ki Saptadhara' — seven pillars for Viksit Bharat — in his 80th Independence Day speech
stories.what_happened: Addressing the nation from the Red Fort on August 15, Prime Minister Narendra Modi unveiled a new organizing framework for India's growth called **'Shakti Ki Saptadhara'** — seven streams of strength he said would power the country's next phase of development. The seven pillars are manufacturing, agriculture and food processing, technology and innovation, **Gati Shakti** (India's infrastructure and logistics connectivity push covering rail, highways, waterways, airports, and ports), defence production, the green and blue economy, and India's cultural soft power. On manufacturing, Modi called for India to become a reliable hub in global supply chains, 'from design to manufacturing.' On defence, he said self-reliance and becoming a global supplier of military hardware was now a national priority. He framed the challenge in stark terms, saying India needed to accomplish in five to seven years what it had not managed in the previous five to seven decades.
key_points: PM Modi unveiled **'Shakti Ki Saptadhara'** (Seven Streams of Strength), naming seven pillars to drive India toward **Viksit Bharat 2047**.
The seven streams: **manufacturing**, agriculture and food processing, technology and innovation, **Gati Shakti** connectivity, defence production, the green and blue economy, and India's soft power.
Modi called for India to become a **reliable global manufacturing hub**, 'from design to manufacturing.'
He set defence production as a priority, saying India must become **self-reliant** and a **global arms supplier**.
Modi said India must achieve in the next **five to seven years** what wasn't achieved in the previous **five to seven decades**.

depth.background: Every Indian Independence Day since 1947 features a prime ministerial address from the ramparts of the **Red Fort** in Delhi, a platform governments use to set the year's political and policy tone. Modi has repeatedly used this speech to frame his government's long-term economic vision, **'Viksit Bharat 2047'** — the goal of making India a fully developed economy by the 100th anniversary of independence. This year's address, his 13th as PM and the nation's 80th Independence Day, built on themes the government had already previewed — a 'Yuva Shakti' (youth power) framing and the revival of the patriotic song 'Vande Mataram' at the ceremony for the first time.

thread.previously: Yesterday's brief covered the government's finalized plans for the ceremony itself — the first-ever singing of 'Vande Mataram' from the Red Fort ramparts, a 2,500-strong human formation spelling the song's name, and an AI-translated broadcast of the PM's speech in over 22 languages.
thread.changed: The ceremony has now happened, and the substance of Modi's speech is known: he used it to unveil 'Shakti Ki Saptadhara,' a new seven-pillar framework for India's growth strategy, rather than just the ceremonial elements previewed yesterday.

stories.title: Modi says India will add 5-8 more semiconductor plants within 7-8 years
stories.what_happened: In his Independence Day address from Delhi's Red Fort, Prime Minister Modi said India has entered 'a new phase' in chip-making, noting that **three plants — run by Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi — have already started commercial production and begun exporting**. He said India could see **another five to eight semiconductor plants become operational over the next seven to eight years**. Officials noted **12 semiconductor projects have been approved across six states**, representing investment commitments exceeding **₹1.64 lakh crore**. Modi's speech came weeks after the government approved **'Semicon 2.0'** in July, a larger **₹1,27,500 crore** program that funds not just chip fabrication but also **chip design, intellectual property and system design** — the higher-value engineering work India has mostly imported until now. He also announced a plan to train **one crore (10 million) young people** in AI skills within a year.
key_points: Three chip plants — **Micron, Kaynes, CG Semi** — are already producing and exporting, Modi said.
India will add **5 to 8 more semiconductor plants** over the next **7-8 years**.
**12 projects** are already approved across six states, worth over **₹1.64 lakh crore** (~$19.5 billion).
A new **'Semicon 2.0'** scheme worth **₹1,27,500 crore** ($15B+) now also funds chip design and IP, not just fabs.
Government will train **1 crore (10 million) youth** in AI skills over the next year.

depth.background: India has spent years trying to break into semiconductor manufacturing — the industry that makes the chips inside every phone, car and data center — an industry dominated by Taiwan, South Korea and the US. Delhi's original semiconductor incentive scheme, launched in 2021-22, offered subsidies to attract fabs; progress was slow at first, with the first approved plants only starting output in the past year or so. On India's **80th Independence Day**, delivering his traditional address from the Red Fort, Modi used the milestone speech to argue the country has now moved from planning to actual production.

stories.title: Modi announces a nationwide talent hunt for kids as young as 5, as India eyes hosting the 2036 Olympics
stories.what_happened: Speaking from the Red Fort on India's **80th Independence Day**, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the country wants to host the **2036 Olympics** and needs to begin preparing now. He announced a **nationwide talent hunt** scouting for sporting ability from village to village, city to city and school to school, focused on children aged **5 to 15**, who would get their abilities assessed and receive specialized training. Modi framed the push as part of a broader seven-point vision he called **"Shakti Ki Saptadhara"** ("seven streams of power") for a **"Viksit Bharat"** (developed India) by 2047, alongside plans to promote India's soft power — yoga, Ayurveda, handicrafts, films, animation and gaming — to draw foreign tourists. It was Modi's **13th consecutive** Independence Day address, making him only the second PM after Jawaharlal Nehru to reach that mark.
key_points: Modi says India is a **strong contender** to host the **2036 Olympics**
A nationwide **talent hunt** will scout children aged **5 to 15** in villages, cities and schools
Scouted kids get **specialized training** to become future Olympic athletes
Announcement came in his **13th consecutive** Independence Day speech, unveiling 'Shakti Ki Saptadhara'

depth.background: India has never hosted an Olympic Games and has historically won very few medals relative to its population — a gap officials blame on weak grassroots talent identification and sports infrastructure. In recent years the government has tried to close that gap through programs like the **Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS)**, which funds elite athletes directly, and **Khelo India**, a broader sports-development initiative. **Ahmedabad** has emerged as India's proposed host city if a 2036 bid goes ahead, and officials say preparation needs to start well over a decade in advance.

stories.title: Modi announces 'next-gen' GST reform as a Diwali gift in his 80th Independence Day speech
stories.source: Press Information Bureau (PIB), Government of India
stories.what_happened: Speaking from the Red Fort on **August 15, India's 80th Independence Day**, PM Modi announced that the government will bring in **'Next-Generation GST reforms'**, explicitly framing them as **'a Diwali gift'** for ordinary citizens by reducing the tax burden on daily-use items. He said the government has prepared a detailed proposal for **broad-based GST rate rationalisation** — meaning fewer, simpler slabs — aimed at making life easier and cheaper for the common man. The ceremony also featured **'Vande Mataram'**, India's national song, performed as part of the official Red Fort programme for the first time since the song was written 150 years ago. Modi's address was his 13th in a row from the ramparts, a run matched only by Jawaharlal Nehru.
key_points: In his **13th consecutive Independence Day speech** from the Red Fort, Modi announced **Next-Generation GST reforms** to cut taxes on everyday goods.
He called the tax cuts a **'Diwali gift'** for citizens, promising the changes will land before the festival season.
The stated goal is to **lower the tax burden on the common man** and boost consumer spending by simplifying GST slabs and rates.
The speech also revived **'Vande Mataram'** in the official Red Fort ceremony for the first time in the song's **150-year history**.
This is Modi's **80th Independence Day** as PM, making him only the **second PM after Nehru** to deliver 13 straight I-Day addresses.

depth.background: **GST (Goods and Services Tax)** is India's main consumption tax, charged on almost everything bought and sold, split across multiple rate 'slabs' (currently ranging roughly 5% to 28%) that businesses and consumers have long complained are confusing and, in places, too high. Simplifying GST has been discussed for years as a way to cut prices for consumers and reduce compliance headaches for small businesses, but slab changes require **agreement between the Centre and states**, since both share GST revenue. Independence Day speeches from the Red Fort are traditionally where Indian prime ministers set the year's policy tone.

sources.name: Press Information Bureau (PIB), Government of India

stories.title: Ukraine hits a Russian rocket factory 900km from the border with its own long-range missile — plus an airbase and an oil terminal in one night
stories.what_happened: In an overnight operation reported Saturday, Ukraine's military struck three targets deep inside Russia using its own weapons. The main hit was on the **Progress Rocket and Space Center** in Samara, roughly **900 kilometers** from the Ukrainian border, using the domestically-produced **Flamingo cruise missile** — Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a direct hit followed by a fire at the site. The same night, Ukrainian forces struck **Savasleyka airbase** in Nizhny Novgorod region (about 700km from the border), which houses MiG-31 jets that Ukraine says are used to launch Kinzhal hypersonic missiles at Ukrainian cities. A third strike hit an oil facility at the port of **Ust-Luga** in Leningrad region, near the Estonian border, where Zelensky said 'necessary damage' was recorded. Zelensky posted on X that the Samara strike used Flamingo missiles and called it 'a good achievement,' adding that Ukraine's campaign to reduce Russia's 'war potential' through long-range strikes is ongoing.
key_points: Ukraine struck the **Progress Rocket and Space Center** in Samara, Russia — **900km** from the Ukrainian border — using its **domestically-built Flamingo cruise missile**.
The same overnight operation also hit **Savasleyka airbase** (home to jets that carry Kinzhal hypersonic missiles) and an **oil terminal at Ust-Luga**, near the Baltic coast.
President **Zelensky** called it a 'good achievement' and said Ukraine's long-range strike campaign against Russia's **war potential** is 'being implemented'.
The target is a state-linked **Roscosmos** facility that makes Soyuz rockets and, Ukraine says, related **electronics** used in Russia's war effort.
It's one of Ukraine's deepest strikes of the war using a weapon it built itself, not one supplied by the US or Europe.

depth.background: Since early 2026, Ukraine has been rolling out the **Flamingo**, its first domestically-produced long-range cruise missile, specifically to strike deep inside Russia without depending on Western-supplied weapons that come with usage restrictions. Progress Rocket and Space Center is one of the flagship factories of **Roscosmos**, Russia's state space agency — historically the maker of the Soyuz rockets that launch astronauts and satellites, but Ukraine says the site also does military-relevant electronics work. This strike lands amid stalled ceasefire diplomacy between Russia, Ukraine, and the US, with both sides still trading long-range blows on infrastructure rather than territory.

stories.title: Israeli settlers still besieging a West Bank village after five days, as analysts explain why Israel hasn't stepped in
stories.what_happened: For **five days**, Palestinians in the West Bank village of **Qusra** — about an hour's drive from Tel Aviv — have been confined to their homes because armed Israeli settlers control the area outside. Despite Israel's military demonstrating, in the same period, its ability to strike targets as far away as **Beirut and Tehran**, it has not fully removed the settlers from Qusra. New analysis published August 15 argues the government's inaction isn't just about Netanyahu's politics — settlers have built deep, mutually reinforcing ties with parts of the military and security establishment, and radical settlers have set up **hundreds of outposts without formal government authorization** while still receiving military protection and public services. Data cited in the reporting shows roughly **190 attacks a month** in the first four months of 2026, putting the West Bank on pace for **more than 2,000 attacks by year's end** — a level the UN called an **"all-time high"** in a July warning. The government has approved new settlements even as the violence has escalated.
key_points: Palestinians in the village of **Qusra** have been trapped in their homes for days, unable to leave because of armed settlers outside.
The **Israeli military** — which has carried out major operations from **Beirut to Tehran** in the past three years — has not removed the settlers.
The **UN warned in July** that West Bank settler violence had hit an **"all-time high."**
Attacks are on pace to exceed **2,000 for the year**, up from about **190 a month** in early 2026.
Analysts say the problem isn't just **Netanyahu** — settlers have deep ties to the military and governing coalition itself.

depth.background: The **occupied West Bank** is Palestinian territory Israel has militarily controlled since 1967; roughly 500,000 Israeli settlers now live there in communities most of the world considers illegal under international law, which Israel disputes. Under Prime Minister **Netanyahu's coalition** — described as the **most nationalist and religious government in Israel's history** — settler numbers and outposts have expanded rapidly, with **over 100 new settlements** established. Settler violence against Palestinian communities has been rising for years, but 2026 has seen a sharp escalation. Yesterday, Israeli settlers were reported to have besieged Palestinian homes for five nights running, prompting a rare US rebuke calling it "terror."

thread.previously: Israeli settlers had besieged Palestinian homes in the West Bank village for five nights, prompting a rare US rebuke that called the violence 'terror.'
thread.changed: The siege in the village of Qusra has continued, and new analysis reveals why: settlers have deep structural ties to Israel's military and government that go beyond Netanyahu personally, with attacks now on pace to hit over 2,000 for the year — a UN-flagged 'all-time high.'

stories.title: A magnitude-7.7 earthquake off Indonesia's Flores Island kills at least 20 and triggers a tsunami warning
stories.what_happened: The quake hit at **5:58am local time on Saturday**, centered about 68km north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province at a shallow depth of 10km. Buildings collapsed across several regencies, and residents described fleeing into the streets as the ground shook, with footage showing panicked crowds running through the port town of **Maumere**. Indonesia's geophysics agency (BMKG) issued a tsunami warning for the surrounding coastline, prompting hundreds to rush to higher ground before the warning was lifted roughly three hours later. Death-toll reports diverged through the day: East Nusa Tenggara's governor initially confirmed **5 deaths**, while a Maumere search-and-rescue official later put the toll at **20 dead**, 6 injured, and 2 still buried, with the number expected to keep changing as rescuers reach cut-off areas. Three aftershocks, up to magnitude 6.1, struck within the first half hour, and about 2,000 people evacuated in the neighboring Nagekeo regency.
key_points: A **magnitude-7.7 earthquake** struck at **5:58am local time** on Saturday, centered 68km north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.
Rescue teams in the port town of **Maumere** report **at least 20 dead**, six injured, and two still trapped under rubble, though the toll is still being confirmed.
Indonesia's meteorology agency issued a **tsunami warning** for nearby coastlines, which was lifted after roughly **three hours**.
**Three aftershocks** — up to **magnitude 6.1** — struck within the first half hour.
About **2,000 residents** in the neighboring Nagekeo regency evacuated to higher ground as buildings collapsed.

depth.background: Indonesia sits on the **Pacific 'Ring of Fire'**, the horseshoe-shaped belt of tectonic boundaries that produces roughly 90% of the world's earthquakes, and the archipelago has suffered several major quakes in recent years, including deadly ones on Sulawesi in 2018 and Flores itself in 2021. Flores was devastated by a **magnitude-7.8 quake and tsunami in 1992** that killed over 2,000 people, so the island's population has lived with this exact risk before. Saturday's quake struck at a shallow depth of **10km**, which tends to produce stronger surface shaking than a deeper quake of the same size. Indonesia's national disaster agency (BNPB) has deployed rescue teams, but landslide-blocked roads on the mountainous island are slowing the response.

stories.title: Bangladesh push Australia to the brink on day three in Darwin as the lead balloons past 200
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh resumed day three of the first Test in **Darwin** in a commanding position after posting **351 for 6** on day two, powered by **Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test century (101 runs)**, an **84 from captain Najmul Hossain Shanto**, a composed 49 from Mominul Haque, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz unbeaten on 32. That total gave Bangladesh a first-innings lead of **153 runs** over Australia's **198 all out**. As Australia batted again in their second innings on day three, the deficit kept growing — by the second session, Australia trailed by **216 runs**, with Marnus Labuschagne and Travis Head at the crease trying to build a partnership and avoid an innings defeat. Josh Hazlewood had taken 2 wickets for Australia's bowling attack the previous day but couldn't stop Bangladesh's lower order from extending the total.
key_points: By session two of **day three**, Australia trailed by **216 runs** in the first Test at Darwin — a huge deficit with the match past its halfway point.
Bangladesh's day two total of **351 for 6** was built on **Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test century (101)** and a gritty **84 from captain Najmul Hossain Shanto**.
Australia's first innings closed at just **198**, meaning Bangladesh's lead was already **153** before day three even started.
Marnus Labuschagne and Travis Head were at the crease trying to steady Australia's second innings as the gap widened further.
This is Bangladesh's **first tour of Australia in years**, and a win — or even a draw — from this position would be one of their **biggest overseas results ever**.

depth.background: Bangladesh have historically struggled on **fast, bouncy Australian pitches**, and playing in **Darwin** — an unusual, tropical Test venue for Australia — adds heat and humidity as extra variables. A five-day **Test match** is decided over four innings (two per side); building a big first-innings lead, as Bangladesh have done here, puts huge pressure on the team batting last because they're chasing a target on a worn pitch. **Marnus Labuschagne** and **Travis Head** are senior, experienced Australian batters whose job on day three was to prevent the deficit from Bangladesh's dominant batting from spiraling further out of control.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill 11 in south Lebanon, the deadliest since the June truce, as Hezbollah vows retaliation
stories.what_happened: Israeli airstrikes hit south Lebanon's Nabatieh district early Saturday, killing at least **11 people** according to Lebanon's health ministry, in what multiple outlets are calling the **deadliest single Israeli strike on Lebanon since the June truce**. Seven people, including three children, died when a house was hit on the outskirts of the village of Ansar; four more were killed in a separate strike on Deir El Zahrani, with 19 people wounded across both sites. Israel's military said it struck 'Hezbollah infrastructure' in the two areas in response to a Hezbollah drone attack a day earlier that wounded three Israeli soldiers — the same event the previous day's reporting described as Israel killing a single Hezbollah commander in retaliation. Lebanon's prime minister dismissed Israel's claim that those killed were legitimate military targets, insisting that managing weapons on Lebanese soil is the state's responsibility, not Israel's to police unilaterally. Hezbollah said the strikes would be 'met with what they deserve,' raising fears of a further tit-for-tat spiral. The exchange comes ahead of a planned eighth round of US-sponsored direct talks between Israel and Lebanon, expected in Rome in early September.
key_points: Israeli airstrikes killed **11 people**, including **three children**, in south Lebanon's Nabatieh district — the deadliest single strike since the **June ceasefire**.
Seven died in a strike on a house in the village of **Ansar**; four more died in a separate strike on **Deir El Zahrani**; 19 people were wounded.
Israel says the strikes hit **Hezbollah infrastructure** in retaliation for a drone attack that wounded three Israeli soldiers a day earlier.
**Hezbollah has vowed retaliation**, and Lebanon's prime minister rejected Israel's framing, saying weapons on Lebanese soil are the state's responsibility alone.
The escalation comes weeks before **an eighth round of US-mediated Israel-Lebanon talks**, planned for Rome in early September.

depth.background: Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group and political party that controls much of south Lebanon, fought a devastating war in 2023-2024 before a **US-brokered ceasefire in June** eased the worst of the fighting. Since then, the truce has been fragile: Israel has continued near-daily strikes it says target Hezbollah's efforts to rebuild, while Hezbollah has mostly held back from major retaliation. The exchange that produced this strike began when a Hezbollah drone wounded three Israeli soldiers — which we reported yesterday alongside Israel's initial, narrower response of killing a single Hezbollah commander. That account has now given way to a much larger civilian toll.

thread.previously: We reported yesterday that a Hezbollah drone wounded three Israeli soldiers in south Lebanon, and that Israel responded by killing a Hezbollah commander.
thread.changed: The Israeli response was far larger than first reported: strikes on two villages killed 11 people, including three children, making it the deadliest single strike since the June truce, and Hezbollah has now vowed retaliation.

stories.title: Cricket Ireland braces for protests as Afghanistan series ends at Stormont, with Amnesty warning against 'Taliban propaganda'
stories.what_happened: Ireland and Afghanistan play the **fifth and final ODI** of their series at **Stormont** today, August 15, with Afghanistan holding a strong lead after outplaying Ireland in earlier matches — including a 92-run win powered by **Ibrahim Zadran's 84**, while Ireland were bowled out for 207 despite fighting knocks from Cade Carmichael and Andy Balbirnie. Ahead of and during the series, **Amnesty International** publicly warned that hosting Afghanistan risked handing the **Taliban a propaganda platform**, and called on Cricket Ireland, its players, and the ICC to speak out on the treatment of Afghan women. Small protests, including demonstrators dressed in burkas, have already gathered outside the grounds during the earlier Stormont matches. **Cricket Ireland and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI)** say dedicated security and policing plans are in place to protect players, staff, and fans while also allowing lawful protest. Cricket Ireland had earlier admitted **'moral discomfort'** about the series but chose to proceed with it, arguing that engagement rather than isolation was the better path.
key_points: Ireland host Afghanistan for the **fifth and final match** of a five-game ODI series at **Stormont in Belfast** today.
**Amnesty International** has warned the fixtures risk being used as **'Taliban propaganda'** and urged Cricket Ireland and the ICC to speak out on Afghan women's rights.
Cricket Ireland says **security plans are in place**, with police confirming a **'proportionate policing plan'** for any demonstrations.
Small protests, including women in burkas, have already taken place outside grounds during earlier matches in the series.
**Afghanistan has dominated the series**, including a 92-run win built on Ibrahim Zadran's 84, leaving Ireland needing a big turnaround.

depth.background: Since the **Taliban retook power in Afghanistan in 2021**, women there have been banned from playing or even watching sport, barred from universities and parks, and — according to rights groups — hunted down if they try to keep playing in secret; many of Afghanistan's former women cricketers fled the country. Under ICC rules a men's team can keep its full-member status as long as it has a men's program, so **Afghanistan's men's team keeps playing internationally** even though its women's team has been effectively erased. That contradiction has made every Afghanistan men's fixture a flashpoint: **Australia and England have both cancelled or avoided bilateral series** against Afghanistan since 2021, while others, including Ireland, have gone ahead. This five-match ODI series began in Bready on the Irish mainland before shifting to Stormont in Belfast for its last three games.

stories.title: Hezbollah drone wounds three Israeli soldiers in south Lebanon; Israel kills a Hezbollah commander in response
stories.what_happened: In the early hours of Saturday, August 15, a Hezbollah operative flew an explosive drone into a position held by Israeli soldiers from the elite **Yahalom combat-engineering unit** on Ali Taher Ridge, seriously wounding an officer and two soldiers. It was the most damaging attack on Israeli troops in the area in months. The Israeli military responded with a **precision airstrike** on the Lebanese village of Al-Ansar, killing **Ali Samir Al-Haj Hassan**, whom Israel identified as a battalion commander in the Radwan Force — Hezbollah's most highly trained combat unit — along with several other Hezbollah operatives. Israel followed up with additional strikes in the wider Nabatieh area, including on the ridge itself, which Israeli officials say sits above a **major underground Hezbollah facility**. Hezbollah has not publicly confirmed or denied carrying out the drone strike.
key_points: A Hezbollah explosive drone hit Israeli troops on the **Ali Taher Ridge** in south Lebanon around **2:30am Saturday**, seriously wounding an officer and two soldiers.
Israel struck back within hours, killing **Ali Samir Al-Haj Hassan**, a battalion commander in Hezbollah's elite **Radwan Force**, plus several other fighters.
The clash happened inside Lebanon, at a hilltop position Israeli troops still occupy **21 months after the November 2024 ceasefire** was supposed to end the war.
Israel also struck the Nabatieh area, hitting ground above a **Hezbollah underground facility** believed to sit beneath the ridge.
It is one of the most serious cross-border exchanges since the ceasefire, and raises fresh doubts about how long the truce can hold.

depth.background: Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militia and political party that controls much of south Lebanon, fought an intense war through 2024 that ended in a **November 2024 ceasefire**. Under that deal, the Lebanese army was supposed to take over security in the south and Israeli troops were meant to withdraw. Israel never fully left — it kept soldiers at five hilltop positions inside Lebanese territory, including **Ali Taher Ridge**, which it says are needed to watch for Hezbollah rebuilding its tunnel and rocket network. Lebanon considers this an ongoing violation of its sovereignty, while Israel has continued near-weekly strikes on people and sites it says are linked to Hezbollah's rearmament.

stories.title: Modi renews his push for women's reservation in Parliament, months after the enabling bill fell short in the Lok Sabha
stories.what_happened: Speaking from the ramparts of the Red Fort on India's 80th Independence Day, Modi devoted part of his address to reviving the women's reservation issue, calling it the **'call of the hour'** for Indian democracy and pointing to the role women already play as elected representatives in panchayats and municipal bodies. He urged **all political parties**, not just his own, to come together and ensure the 33% quota actually gets implemented in the Lok Sabha and state legislatures. He framed the delay as decades of political **'akhada'** (wrestling-ring) manoeuvring, saying the issue had been stuck in this back-and-forth for roughly **40 years** before Parliament finally passed the underlying law in 2023. The speech came four months after his own government's follow-up bill to activate that law failed in the Lok Sabha in April 2026, falling well short of the two-thirds threshold and forcing two connected bills to be withdrawn. The Congress-led opposition did not respond to the substance of the appeal; instead, sparring on Independence Day centred on other issues, including the Leader of the Opposition's absence from the Red Fort ceremony and the government's record on women's safety.
key_points: In his 80th Independence Day speech, Modi called **33% reservation for women** in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies the **'call of the hour'** and urged every political party to back it.
The reservation law already exists on paper — the **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam** took legal effect in **April 2026** — but it cannot actually seat a single woman yet.
The follow-up bill needed to switch it on, the **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026**, fell **54 votes short** of the two-thirds majority it needed in the Lok Sabha this April.
Because that vote failed, real implementation now waits on the **2027 census** and a fresh redrawing of constituency boundaries, pushing actual women's seats out to roughly **2034**.
Modi accused the opposition of stalling the issue for **'four decades'**; Congress did not engage directly and instead hit back on unrelated fronts.

depth.background: India has debated a law reserving one-third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women since the mid-1990s, with multiple bills introduced and lapsing over nearly three decades. Parliament finally passed the **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam** (the 106th Constitutional Amendment) in 2023, and it formally came into force on **16 April 2026** — but the law itself said the quota could only kick in *after* the next delimitation, the redrawing of constituency boundaries based on fresh census data. To trigger that delimitation early, the government brought the **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** to the Lok Sabha this April, alongside a Delimitation Bill and a Union Territories Laws Amendment Bill. That attempt collapsed: the bill won only **298 of the 352 votes** required for the constitutionally mandated two-thirds special majority, forcing the government to withdraw the two dependent bills as well.

stories.title: Mount Etna's eruption shuts Sicily's main airport for a sixth straight day, with ash reaching Libya
stories.what_happened: A new eruptive sequence began at Etna's Voragine crater around August 6-7, with Strombolian activity (small, frequent bursts of lava and gas) intensifying through the evening and evolving into sustained lava fountaining. Ash columns rose high enough to force repeated, rolling suspensions of all arrivals and departures at Catania airport, with authorities extending the closure day after day as the volcano kept erupting rather than settling down. By mid-week the shutdown had been extended through the early hours of Saturday, August 15, and hundreds of diverted flights were straining smaller airports in Palermo, Trapani, Comiso and Lamezia Terme. INGV scientists noted this is the volcano's second intense paroxysmal episode within a month, following one in late July, with new lateral fissures opening at lower elevations — a sign the activity is more complex than a routine paroxysm.
key_points: Europe's most active volcano has been erupting since **August 6-7**, forcing Sicily's Catania airport — Italy's **fifth-busiest** by passenger traffic — to suspend all flights for a **sixth consecutive day**.
More than **1,350 flights** have been disrupted in the past week; **36%** of nearly 2,000 scheduled arrivals between Aug 6-12 were cancelled and over **600** diverted to other airports.
The ash plume has drifted as far as Malta and **Libya**, hundreds of kilometers from the volcano, triggering aviation red alerts.
Estimated tourism-related losses for Sicily range from **€12 million to €24 million**, hitting hotels, restaurants, taxis and tour operators at the height of summer travel season.

Italy's INGV volcanology institute says this is the **second major paroxysmal sequence in under a month**, with lava fountains and new lateral fissures making the eruption's endpoint hard to predict; the closure was extended again into the early hours of August 15.

depth.background: Mount Etna, on Sicily's east coast, is Europe's tallest and most continuously active volcano, prone to short bursts called "paroxysms" — episodes of intense lava fountaining and ash emission from its summit craters. Catania's Fontanarossa airport sits directly in the volcano's shadow and has been repeatedly closed by ashfall in past eruptions, including as recently as 2024. Sicily depends heavily on this single gateway airport for its peak-season tourism economy, handling over **12 million passengers in 2025**.

stories.title: Venezuela frees 131 more political prisoners as post-Maduro transition talks continue
stories.what_happened: Venezuela's interim government said on Friday it had freed **131** more people it classifies as political prisoners, bringing the total released since Maduro's removal to **1,046**, according to US Secretary of State **Marco Rubio**. The releases were carried out under a program called the "Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence," with detainees granted "alternative measures from incarceration" rather than formal pardons. Rubio called it "a crucial step for the nation's reconciliation process" in a post on X. But opposition party Vente Venezuela said it could independently confirm only 43 releases, and rights group Foro Penal put the verified number at "at least 40" — well short of the government's claim. Foro Penal separately reported that **391** political prisoners, including both civilians and military personnel, remained behind bars as of August 10. Opposition figure Juan Pablo Guanipa welcomed the releases but demanded the government free everyone still detained.
key_points: Venezuela freed **131** more political prisoners on Friday.
Total released since Maduro's ouster now stands at **1,046**.
Releases fall under the **"Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence"**.
Opposition groups could independently verify only **40–43** releases.
**391** political prisoners remained jailed as of August 10.

depth.background: In January 2026, US forces removed and detained Venezuelan leader **Nicolás Maduro**, ending his long rule and opening a fragile political transition. Since then, the interim government has framed releasing political prisoners — people jailed mainly for opposing the old regime — as proof it's serious about reconciliation. Independent rights groups like **Foro Penal** track releases separately because government figures have been hard to confirm on their own. Washington has treated the pace of releases as a benchmark for how much it eases pressure on Caracas.

stories.title: US and Canada hold near-daily talks as Ottawa balks at Washington's tariff offer, three days from a 50% deadline
stories.what_happened: With the tariff deadline now just three days out, Canada's chief negotiator **Janice Charette** and cabinet minister **Dominic LeBlanc** told officials that talks would continue through the weekend, with LeBlanc saying Canada would hold **'as many meetings as it takes.'** Despite the intensity, Canadian officials say there remains significant work left to reach an agreement, and Canada is **not satisfied** with the most recent offer from Washington. Unresolved issues include eliminating Canada's retaliatory auto tariffs, lifting provincial restrictions on American alcohol sales, and reworking dairy quota arrangements. Canadian and US officials are hoping to have a deal framework in front of Trump before Wednesday, though Team Canada believes he has **not yet been fully briefed** on the state of play.
key_points: Canadian negotiators say they'll hold **'as many meetings as it takes'** before Wednesday's deadline.
The threatened tariffs would hit a wide range of Canadian goods — including **dairy, alcohol, hockey sticks, cement and electronics** — at a **50% rate**.
Canada says it is **not satisfied** with the latest US offer; sticking points include **auto tariffs, alcohol-sale rules and dairy quotas**.
Canadian officials believe **Trump has not yet been personally briefed** on the state of the talks, adding uncertainty just days out.

depth.background: Earlier this year President Trump threatened a fresh **50% tariff** on a broad swath of Canadian goods, layered on top of tariffs he had already imposed on Canadian steel, aluminum, copper, autos and lumber. Talks have run for weeks between Canadian trade officials and their US counterparts, with Canadian Prime Minister **Mark Carney's** government under domestic pressure to land a deal that protects key industries like dairy and autos without giving up too much ground.

thread.previously: We reported that Canada and the US were racing to strike a trade deal before President Trump's threatened 50% tariff on a broad range of Canadian goods was set to hit on Wednesday.
thread.changed: With the deadline now just three days away, Canada's negotiating team — Dominic LeBlanc and Janice Charette — say they'll hold 'as many meetings as it takes,' but Canada remains **unsatisfied with the latest US offer**, and Canadian officials believe **Trump himself has not yet been briefed** on where talks stand.

stories.title: Modi's Independence Day flagship: AI-skill training for 1 crore youth within a year
stories.what_happened: Speaking from the ramparts of the Red Fort on India's 80th Independence Day, Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** announced that the government would provide AI-skill training to **1 crore (10 million) youth over the next year**, framing it as key to India leading in the AI era. The announcement came alongside other youth-focused measures, including free coaching support, as part of a speech that referenced youth more than 50 times. It represents a dramatic scale-up: government data shows only about **53,449 candidates** had enrolled in AI-related job roles under the existing PMKVY 4.0 scheme as of June 30, 2026, with roughly **25,466 certified** so far.
key_points: Modi announced AI-skill training for **1 crore (10 million) youth** within the **next one year**.
It was the centerpiece of his **80th Independence Day** address from the Red Fort, which mentioned 'youth' more than **50 times** in a 75-minute speech.
It's a huge scale-up from the government's existing AI-skilling track — **PMKVY 4.0** had enrolled just **~53,449 candidates** as of June 30, 2026.
The stated goal: equip Indian youth to **'lead the world'** in artificial intelligence as the technology reshapes jobs globally.

depth.background: India's flagship skilling program, the **Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY)**, has run for a decade training workers in trades from electronics to hospitality, and now includes an AI-focused track under its fourth phase. The announcement lands against a backdrop of rising anxiety over AI's effect on jobs worldwide, and domestically amid ongoing protests in states like Jharkhand over exam and recruitment irregularities that have left many young job-seekers frustrated.

stories.title: Suryakumar Yadav trade buzz builds: reports link MI star to KKR in a possible Shreyas Iyer swap
stories.what_happened: Speculation about Yadav's IPL future first picked up in June, when former India wicketkeeper Robin Uthappa suggested on a YouTube show that Yadav could return to KKR, possibly to work again under Gautam Gambhir. That early wave alone had gone cold, but a fresh report on 15 August — explicitly framed as an update ahead of the IPL 2027 trade window and auction — reignited the story: multiple outlets reported that KKR made an informal approach to Mumbai Indians, with one structure being discussed involving **Shreyas Iyer moving to MI** as part of the exchange, notable given Iyer is the man who replaced Yadav as India's T20I captain. Yadav's underwhelming IPL 2026 season, in which Mumbai Indians missed the playoffs, has added weight to the talk that the franchise may be open to moving him on. As of the latest report, neither club nor the player has made any public statement confirming a trade request or an agreed deal — this remains reported speculation, not a done deal.
key_points: Reports say KKR have held informal talks to **trade for** Suryakumar Yadav
One version of the deal reportedly sends **Shreyas Iyer** to MI in return
Comes months after Yadav was **stripped of India's T20I captaincy**, replaced by Iyer
Yadav managed only around **200 runs** across IPL 2026 as MI missed the playoffs
**No official confirmation** yet from MI, KKR, or Yadav himself

depth.background: Suryakumar Yadav started his IPL career at Kolkata Knight Riders from **2014 to 2017**, winning the title with them in 2014, before Mumbai Indians signed him and he became one of India's premier T20 batters. He was later made India's T20I captain and led the team to the **2026 T20 World Cup title** — but weeks later was removed from the captaincy after a poor run of form, with **Shreyas Iyer** named his replacement. IPL teams can privately negotiate player trades during an open **trade window** before each season's auction; this year's window has been open since around June 2026.

stories.title: Cadillac's new boss says cracking Ferrari's engine secrets is the key to ending a winless run
stories.what_happened: In his first detailed remarks since taking over, new Cadillac team principal Marcin Budkowski pinpointed exactly where he thinks the team is losing time: understanding the 'intricacies' of energy management on its Ferrari power unit. Budkowski said engine suppliers do not always hand customer teams 'all the tricks of the trade,' calling that simply 'part of the game' in F1. He pointed to **McLaren** as his model — that team started 2026 complaining it lacked full information from Mercedes about the new-era engine, yet went on to win the **Hungarian Grand Prix** once it closed that knowledge gap. Cadillac's two drivers, Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, remain without a single World Championship point after 11 rounds of the team's debut season. Budkowski, who officially takes charge at the Dutch Grand Prix on August 21-23, is framing better communication with Ferrari — not new car parts — as the fastest route to Cadillac's first points.
key_points: Marcin Budkowski replaced Graeme Lowdon as Cadillac boss just days ago
Cadillac has scored **zero points** through 11 rounds this season
Budkowski wants to master Ferrari's **energy management** tricks
He cites McLaren's Hungarian GP win as proof it can work
His first race in charge is the Dutch GP on **August 21-23**

depth.background: F1's redesigned 2026 rules brought all-new **power units** (the combined engine-plus-battery system) that lean far more heavily on electrical energy than before, so how a team manages that energy across a lap has become a genuine performance differentiator. Cadillac is F1's newest team, backed by General Motors, and it races with **Ferrari-supplied engines** rather than building its own — a common F1 arrangement known as being a 'customer team.' Cadillac abruptly sacked team boss Graeme Lowdon this week and replaced him with F1 veteran **Marcin Budkowski**, whose past stops include Ferrari, McLaren, the FIA and Renault/Alpine.

stories.title: Iran and Oman edge closer to a Hormuz shipping-map deal even as attacks on tankers keep mounting
stories.what_happened: Bloomberg reported on August 15 that Iran and Oman are homing in on a deal to manage traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, even as attacks on ships in the region continue to increase the pressure to act. The two sides have already agreed on the **geographic coordinates** of a safe route ships can use, plus a plan for a **joint coordination center** that would monitor which vessels pass through. Iran's Foreign Ministry has stressed this is a **sovereign, bilateral arrangement with Oman** — not a resolution of its standoff with Washington. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has repeated that a deal with Oman alone won't fully reopen the strait to commercial shipping; Iran still wants concessions, including **compensation from the United States**, before that happens. The technical progress comes even as ship attacks in the wider Gulf region have been rising, adding urgency to finding at least a partial fix.
key_points: Iran and Oman have now agreed on the **geographic coordinates** of a safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz.
The two countries also plan a **joint coordination center** to monitor vessel traffic through the strait.
Iran says this Oman-brokered technical fix is a **separate track** from its wider dispute with the US and won't by itself reopen the strait.
Tehran is still demanding **compensation from Washington** before shipping fully resumes, even as ship attacks in the region increase.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is a narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that roughly **one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil** passes through every day — it is the only sea route out of the Persian Gulf for major oil exporters like Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and the UAE. Iran has kept the strait effectively closed to a lot of traffic since the US and Israel went to war with it in February 2026, and the standoff has now run past **five months**. Ten days ago, Iran's Supreme Leader installed a hardliner, Mohsen Rezaei, to run the security council that oversees exactly these decisions — a sign Tehran wasn't in a rush to make concessions.

thread.previously: On August 10, Iran's Supreme Leader appointed hardliner Mohsen Rezaei to run its security council, even as Foreign Minister Araghchi said a Hormuz deal with Oman was 'very close' — though he cautioned a deal with Oman alone wouldn't fully reopen the strait without US concessions.
thread.changed: The two sides have now actually agreed on the concrete details: the geographic coordinates of a safe shipping route and a joint coordination center to monitor traffic — real technical progress, even as ship attacks in the region keep rising.
