stories.title: India will play their 600th Test — the first Asian team to reach the milestone — as the Sri Lanka series opens at Galle
stories.what_happened: India's first Test against Sri Lanka, starting **August 15** at Galle International Stadium, will be India's **600th Test match overall**, making them the first Asian side and just the third team in history — after England and Australia — to reach that number. The match is also the **50th Test hosted at Galle**, the first Asian venue to reach that mark. Captain **Shubman Gill**, who described the milestone as a 'huge honour,' will lead a squad that includes vice-captain KL Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Rishabh Pant, Ravindra Jadeja, and uncapped seamer **Auqib Nabi**, who earned a shock maiden call-up after **Jasprit Bumrah** was ruled out with a knee injury. Sri Lanka will field a 16-member squad led by Dhananjaya de Silva, with Kamindu Mendis as his deputy. The two-match series runs through late August.
key_points: India become the **first Asian team**, and only the **third team ever**, to play **600 Tests**.
The Galle Test is also the **50th Test match** ever played at that ground — a first for any Asian venue.
Captain **Shubman Gill** called leading the side in this Test a **'huge honour and privilege.'**
India's squad includes **Auqib Nabi**, uncapped, called up after **Jasprit Bumrah** was ruled out injured.
The first of two Tests runs **August 15–19** at Galle International Stadium.

depth.background: Only England and Australia had previously reached 600 Test matches — a mark of just how long and central those two nations have been to the format since Test cricket began in 1877. India, despite a huge domestic cricket culture, is reaching this landmark later because Test cricket globally has always been dominated in volume by England and Australia's early head start. Galle, meanwhile, has become one of world cricket's most picturesque and historic grounds since Sri Lanka started hosting Tests there, set beside the Indian Ocean next to a centuries-old Dutch fort.

stories.title: Bar Council of India reverses order that would have barred NALSAR's 2026 graduates from becoming lawyers, after backlash
stories.what_happened: On August 13, the BCI Chairman issued a direction barring all State Bar Councils from enrolling NALSAR's 2026 graduating batch as advocates, citing the campaign against CJI Surya Kant's convocation invitation. The order sparked immediate backlash, including from legal circles who called it a disproportionate collective punishment. Within about an hour of the initial fallout, the full BCI Council met, reviewed the matter, and concluded that most of the graduating students were innocent of any intent to protest the CJI's invitation. The Council formally withdrew the Chairman's enrolment ban, clearing all 2026 NALSAR graduates to enrol with their chosen State Bar Council. BCI said it will still wait for a formal inquiry report from NALSAR's Vice-Chancellor before deciding on any further action against those actually responsible.
key_points: The **Bar Council of India (BCI)** withdrew, within about an hour, its own order barring **NALSAR University of Law's 2026 graduates** from enrolling as advocates.
The original order followed a row over inviting **Chief Justice Surya Kant** to NALSAR's convocation, which some students reportedly opposed.
BCI said the **'vast majority' of students were innocent** and had not intended to campaign against the CJI's invitation.
All 2026 NALSAR graduates can now enrol with the **State Bar Council** of their choice.
BCI will still await an **inquiry report** from NALSAR's Vice-Chancellor before deciding on further action.

depth.background: NALSAR University of Law in Hyderabad is one of India's most prestigious national law schools. A controversy erupted after some students reportedly campaigned against Chief Justice of India Surya Kant being invited as chief guest to their convocation. BCI Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra responded on August 13 by directing State Bar Councils not to enrol any NALSAR 2026 graduate as an advocate — a career-ending threat for an entire graduating class over the actions of some students.

stories.title: Russia says it's ready to resume Ukraine peace talks — but only to discuss Washington's plan, not a multi-party one
stories.what_happened: Grigory Karasin, chairman of the Russian Federation Council's foreign affairs committee, said Thursday that Russia is ready to resume peace talks on ending the war in Ukraine. He specified that Moscow's negotiators are prepared to discuss the **new proposals brought by the US**, and see **no obstacles** to a meeting with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Karasin added a pointed condition: Russia wants to consider proposals **from one side — Washington — rather than a combined plan from multiple parties**, an apparent swipe at attempts to bring Ukraine and European governments into the same drafting process. The statement doesn't set a date or format for any meeting, and doesn't walk back Russia's core demand that Ukraine hand over the remainder of the Donbas region it still controls, a demand Kyiv has repeatedly rejected. It comes after weeks in which Russian officials, including Lavrov, downplayed the urgency of a return to the table.
key_points: Grigory Karasin, who chairs the Russian upper house's foreign affairs committee, says Moscow has **no obstacles** to meeting US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The catch: Russia wants to discuss **only the new US proposals**, not a plan negotiated with Ukraine and Europe at the table too.
This follows months where Russia's chief negotiators played down or stalled on restarting talks entirely.
No date or venue has been confirmed yet for any Witkoff-Kushner meeting with Russian officials.
Russia's underlying territorial demand — that Ukraine cede the rest of Donbas — has **not changed**.

depth.background: The US has been running a parallel diplomatic track to the stalled Istanbul-framework talks, with **Steve Witkoff** (Trump's special envoy) and **Jared Kushner** shuttling proposals between Washington, Kyiv and Moscow. Russia spent much of the summer signaling it was in no rush to talk, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov repeatedly rejecting a front-line freeze as a precondition. Ukraine, meanwhile, has said it's ready to talk but needs clarity on what the Kremlin's actual terms are, since Russian officials have often floated different demands in different forums. **Karasin's comments** are the clearest recent signal that Moscow sees the direct Washington-run channel, not a broader multilateral one, as the venue it's willing to use.

stories.title: Trent Rockets reach both Hundred finals as men's Eliminator between Manchester Super Giants and Sunrisers Leeds looms at the Oval
stories.what_happened: Trent Rockets have already locked in their place in both the men's and women's Hundred finals at Lord's on August 16, after topping their respective group tables. In the men's competition, the battle for the second final spot comes down to Friday's Eliminator at The Oval between Manchester Super Giants and Sunrisers Leeds — the same two sides who met just days earlier, when Manchester's big win pulled them level with Sunrisers on 20 points and ahead on net run-rate, securing the higher Eliminator seeding. On the women's side, Trent Rockets sealed top spot with 28 points from eight group matches, meaning they progress straight to Sunday's final without playing in an Eliminator.
key_points: **Trent Rockets** have already secured their place in both the men's and women's Hundred finals at Lord's on **August 16**.
In the men's competition, **Manchester Super Giants** face **Sunrisers Leeds** in Friday's Eliminator at The Oval, with the winner also advancing to the final.
Manchester Super Giants reached the Eliminator after a big win over Sunrisers Leeds on Tuesday, edging them into second place on **net run-rate**.
Trent Rockets' women's side automatically qualified for Sunday's final after topping their table with **28 points** from eight group games.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-format franchise cricket competition, running both men's and women's tournaments in parallel each August. Teams play a round-robin group stage, after which the top side goes straight to the final while the second- and third-placed teams meet in a knockout Eliminator for the other final spot.

thread.previously: We reported that Sunrisers Leeds had reached the Eliminator stage after Birmingham Phoenix's win eliminated MI London.
thread.changed: Manchester Super Giants have since beaten Sunrisers Leeds directly to claim the higher Eliminator seeding, meaning the two sides now face off again today for the final spot in Sunday's final — while Trent Rockets have locked in both the men's and women's final berths.

stories.title: Houthi attack on Yemen's al-Makha port kills at least four, as fighting spreads beyond Taiz
stories.what_happened: Yemen's government said a Houthi attack on **al-Makha and its port killed at least four people**, according to reporting from Al Jazeera on August 14. The Houthi-run SABA news agency separately claimed its forces struck a Saudi Aramco facility in the Saudi border city of **Najran** with a drone. The attacks follow a rise in hostilities between the Houthis and Yemen's government, and come alongside reports that a Houthi assault on a position near the Saudi-Yemen border, held by Sudanese paramilitary troops fighting as part of the Saudi-led coalition, killed **six Sudanese soldiers**. Fighting has also been reported in Taiz, a separate front further inland. The pattern suggests a broadening, not a narrowing, of active combat across multiple fronts simultaneously.
key_points: Yemen's internationally-recognised government says a Houthi attack on the port city of **al-Makha killed at least four people**.
It comes as Houthi rebels also claimed a **drone strike on a Saudi Aramco facility** in Najran, just across the Saudi border.
The attack widens a front that was already active in **Taiz**, where Houthi and government forces have been clashing.
It follows a broader pattern: Houthi attacks on the Saudi-Yemen border have reportedly killed **Sudanese coalition troops** stationed there in recent days.
The escalation comes as **US-Iran diplomacy remains stalled**, with Iran demanding sanctions relief and a US troop withdrawal from the region.

depth.background: Yemen has been fractured since 2014 between the **Houthi movement** (which controls the north, including the capital Sanaa, and is backed by Iran) and Yemen's internationally-recognised government (backed by a **Saudi-led coalition**). A fragile, on-and-off truce has held for stretches over the past two years, but fighting has flared repeatedly, especially as the wider Middle East has grown tenser this year over the standoff around the Strait of Hormuz. Al-Makha (also spelled Mokha) is a strategic Red Sea port city — control of Yemen's coastline matters because Houthi forces have also used it to threaten shipping through one of the world's busiest sea lanes.

stories.title: Cricket Australia and players' union clash over urgency of stalled BBL pay and privatisation talks
stories.what_happened: Cricket Australia and the Australian Cricketers' Association remain **not aligned** on the urgency of resolving BBL player contracting, according to ESPNcricinfo. CA CEO Todd Greenberg said the organisation is still negotiating a pay deal with the ACA while simultaneously discussing the broader **privatisation** of BBL franchises, with hopes of making progress by September. A **contracting embargo** remains in place, leaving both teams and players uncertain about the season ahead; five senior players have reportedly rejected Australian central contracts due to pay disparities, and others are reportedly still weighing whether to play in the BBL at all. Greenberg acknowledged CA **"should have done a better job"** publicly explaining why bringing in private capital is necessary — arguing that without significantly higher salary-cap spending, Australia risks losing its best players to richer overseas T20 leagues.
key_points: Cricket Australia (CA) and the **Australian Cricketers' Association (ACA)** are not aligned on how urgently a BBL pay deal is needed.
CA CEO **Todd Greenberg** says the board is still negotiating pay terms and discussing **privatisation** with Big Bash franchises.
A **contracting embargo** has left teams and players in limbo ahead of the new BBL season.
**Five senior players reportedly rejected** Australian central contracts over pay disparities.
Greenberg admits CA "should have done a better job" explaining why private capital is needed to keep the league competitive.

depth.background: The Big Bash League (BBL) is Australia's flagship men's domestic T20 competition. Cricket Australia has been pushing a plan to sell private-equity stakes in BBL franchises — similar to moves in other T20 leagues worldwide — arguing it's needed to raise player salary caps and keep Australia's best players from being lured away by richer overseas leagues. But the plan has faced pushback, including from states like New South Wales and Queensland who rejected an earlier version of the private-capital proposal, and from the players' union over how any new money would be shared.

stories.title: Melbourne Renegades name Australia assistant coach Gavan Twining as new WBBL head coach
stories.what_happened: The Melbourne Renegades have appointed **Gavan Twining**, currently an assistant coach with Australia's national women's team, as their new WBBL head coach ahead of the upcoming season (WBBL 12). Twining has been part of the Australian set-up since late 2024 and was involved in the team's **Women's T20 World Cup** win in England this year. At the Renegades, he will work with national captain **Sophie Molineux** and leg-spin all-rounder **Georgia Wareham**. Twining will join the Renegades camp after Australia's upcoming series against Bangladesh and New Zealand concludes, and will return to the Australian team once the WBBL season finishes, juggling both roles.
key_points: **Gavan Twining**, an Australia women's team assistant coach, is the Renegades' new WBBL head coach.
He replaces **Simon Helmot**, who stepped down in April to pursue overseas franchise-league coaching roles.
Twining played a role in Australia winning this year's **Women's T20 World Cup** in England.
He'll reunite with Renegades stars **Sophie Molineux** (national captain) and **Georgia Wareham**.
Twining joins after Australia's series against **Bangladesh and New Zealand**, and returns to the national set-up after **WBBL 12** ends.

depth.background: The Women's Big Bash League (WBBL) is Australia's premier domestic Twenty20 women's cricket competition, now heading into its 12th season. The Melbourne Renegades are one of eight WBBL franchises. Their previous coach, Simon Helmot, led the team to a championship before leaving in April for opportunities coaching in overseas T20 franchise leagues, which have multiplied globally and now compete with national federations for coaching talent.

stories.title: Guyana Amazon Warriors open their CPL 2026 title bid with a comfortable win over Jamaica Kingsmen
stories.what_happened: **Guyana Amazon Warriors** began their **Caribbean Premier League (CPL) 2026** campaign with a six-wicket win over **Jamaica Kingsmen** at Sabina Park, Kingston. Put in to bowl first, Guyana bundled Jamaica out for just **117**, with **Mohammad Nabi** returning figures of **4 wickets** to rip through the middle order. Guyana then chased the target down comfortably, with **Shai Hope unbeaten on 56** off 41 balls anchoring the run-chase alongside contributions from Nabi and Quentin Sampson. The result put the Amazon Warriors top of the early CPL table and extended Jamaica Kingsmen's losing run to **three matches** from three this season. Guyana fielded a heavily overseas-stocked squad this year, including Afghanistan all-rounder Nabi, New Zealand's Glenn Phillips, and South Africa's Imran Tahir and Dwaine Pretorius, giving the team an experienced core to build a title push around.
key_points: **Guyana Amazon Warriors** bowled out Jamaica Kingsmen for just **117** to open their CPL 2026 campaign.
**Mohammad Nabi** took **4 wickets**, and **Shai Hope's unbeaten 56** sealed the chase.
The win put Guyana **top of the early CPL 2026 table**.
**Jamaica Kingsmen** have now **lost all three** of their matches this season.

depth.background: The Caribbean Premier League is the Caribbean's flagship T20 franchise competition, running annually since 2013 and expanded to **seven teams** for 2026. Guyana Amazon Warriors built a strong overseas contingent this season specifically to chase the title, pairing Caribbean talent with experienced international players like Nabi, Phillips, Tahir and Pretorius.

stories.title: A tunnel collapses at a Himalayan hydropower project in Uttarakhand, killing at least 7 workers
stories.what_happened: On the evening of **August 13**, a landslide is believed to have sent a sudden surge of water and debris into the under-construction tail race tunnel at the Pipalkoti hydroelectric project site in Chamoli district, while workers inside were welding reinforcement bars. Of **28 workers on duty**, **22 were trapped** when the collapse happened. At least **7 workers have been confirmed dead** and around **14 injured**; rescue teams managed to pull a number of survivors out, though a handful of workers remained missing as of the latest reports. Disaster response teams from the NDRF, SDRF, ITBP (Indo-Tibetan Border Police) and fire services have been working through rising water and debris inside the tunnel to reach anyone still trapped.
key_points: At least **7 workers killed** and around **14 injured** after a tunnel collapse in Chamoli district.
**22 of 28 workers** on duty were trapped when water and debris suddenly flooded the tunnel.
A **landslide** is believed to have triggered the inrush while workers were welding reinforcement bars.
**NDRF, ITBP and fire services** are racing to reach a small number of workers still missing.
The tunnel belongs to the **Vishnugad-Pipalkoti Hydroelectric Project** on the Alaknanda river.

depth.background: Uttarakhand's Himalayan valleys are dotted with under-construction hydropower tunnels because the state's steep, fast-flowing rivers are ideal for generating electricity — but the same young, fragile mountains make tunnelling there unusually dangerous. The region has a grim recent history: the 2021 Tapovan disaster and the 2023 Silkyara tunnel collapse (where 41 workers were trapped for 17 days) both happened in comparable hydropower or highway tunnels nearby. This latest collapse struck the **Tail Race Tunnel (TRT)** of the **Vishnugad-Pipalkoti Hydroelectric Project**, run by state-run **THDC (Tehri Hydro Development Corporation) Limited**, with construction handled by Hindustan Construction Company (HCC).

stories.title: Wall Street's S&P 500 closes at a fresh record as cooling inflation and falling oil prices lift stocks
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, fresh US inflation data came in **softer than economists expected**, easing fears that the Fed would need to keep rates high for longer. At the same time, oil prices retreated from their recent spike, taking pressure off transport and energy costs that feed into broader inflation. Together, the two moves pushed the **S&P 500 to a new closing record of 7,798.99**, a 0.7% gain, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 69.72 points (0.13%) to 53,839.99 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.81% to 26,803.03. It marks the second time in roughly a week the S&P has set a fresh all-time high.
key_points: The **S&P 500** closed at a record **7,798.99**, up 0.7% on the day.
The **Dow Jones** rose to **53,839.99** and the **Nasdaq** gained 0.8% to **26,803.03**.
The rally was driven by a **cooler-than-expected US inflation report** and **falling oil prices**.
It is the index's second fresh record in two weeks, extending a **booming 2026 rally**.

depth.background: US stocks have been on a strong run through 2026, helped by a Federal Reserve under new chair **Kevin Warsh** that has kept interest rates steady even as some officials push for hikes. Inflation — the pace at which prices for everyday goods rise — has been the market's biggest worry all year, because faster inflation usually means higher interest rates, which make borrowing costlier for companies and consumers alike. Oil prices have also been volatile because of the standoff over the **Strait of Hormuz**, a narrow shipping chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil.

stories.title: Israel kills a Hamas commander in Gaza's first deadly strikes in over a week, straining the fragile ceasefire
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, an Israeli strike in **Khan Younis** killed Hudhaifa Khaled Suleiman Qawari, whom the IDF described as a commander in Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade involved in training fighters, moving weapons and rebuilding the group's capabilities. Hours later, a **drone fired three missiles** at a vehicle on al-Rashid Street southwest of Gaza City, killing Colonel Jamal Abu Kamil, a 43-year-old senior official in Gaza's Hamas-run police force, and injuring two others. Gaza's health ministry said these were the **first combat deaths in more than a week**, during which Israel had scaled back strikes under US pressure while disarmament talks continued. The IDF says both men were 'advancing attacks' on Israeli troops, which it argues justifies action even inside the ceasefire. Israeli forces now hold roughly **70% of Gaza's territory**, up sharply from the ceasefire's early weeks.
key_points: The IDF killed **Hudhaifa Khaled Suleiman Qawari**, a Hamas Khan Younis Brigade commander, in a Thursday strike.
A **separate drone strike** killed a senior Gaza police official, **Colonel Jamal Abu Kamil**, and wounded two others.
These are the **first fatalities in more than a week**, breaking a rare lull under the October 2025 ceasefire.
Israeli control of Gaza territory has grown from about **53% in October to nearly 70% today**.
Hamas has formally accepted a **15-point US-backed roadmap** to disarm, but continued strikes cast doubt on it.

depth.background: A ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect in **October 2025**, ending the most intense phase of the Gaza war, but it was never a full peace — Israeli forces stayed inside parts of Gaza and the two sides never agreed on Hamas's disarmament. A US-backed 'Board of Peace' and an International Stabilization Force have been pushing a follow-on roadmap: Hamas gives up its weapons in phases while Israel gradually withdraws. Hamas said yes to the roadmap on paper, but on the ground Israel has kept carrying out strikes it says are pre-emptive, and its footprint inside Gaza has quietly kept expanding rather than shrinking.

stories.title: India cruise past Sri Lanka Cricket XI in their Galle warm-up as bowling coach Morkel backs KL Rahul to anchor the Test series
stories.what_happened: India opened their Sri Lanka tour with a comfortable **six-wicket win over a Sri Lanka Cricket XI** in a three-day warm-up match, built around an unbeaten **142 from Devdutt Padikkal**. In the build-up, India's bowling coach Morne Morkel spoke publicly about the value KL Rahul brings to the squad, highlighting his experience and his role in helping younger players adjust to conditions in Sri Lanka. Rahul trained alongside captain Shubman Gill, Padikkal and Rishabh Pant in pre-match sessions at the Galle International Stadium, where the first of two Tests begins on **August 15**. The warm-up win gives India momentum heading into a series where they are already missing frontline pace bowler Jasprit Bumrah.
key_points: India beat a **Sri Lanka Cricket XI by six wickets** in their three-day warm-up match, with **Devdutt Padikkal scoring an unbeaten 142**.
India's bowling coach **Morne Morkel** publicly backed **KL Rahul** to play a key role in the upcoming Test series.
Rahul is the **sole survivor** from India's batting group on their last tour of Sri Lanka in 2017, giving him rare experience in these conditions.
Captain **Shubman Gill trained alongside Rahul, Padikkal and Rishabh Pant** in pre-match sessions at Galle International Stadium.
The first Test against Sri Lanka begins **August 15 in Galle**, with India missing Jasprit Bumrah to injury.

depth.background: India's tour of Sri Lanka comes at a moment when the squad is already carrying significant injury concerns — Jasprit Bumrah was ruled out with a knee issue, and captain Shubman Gill has also been managing a finger injury heading into the series. KL Rahul, a senior and experienced batter, is the only player left in India's current squad who also featured on India's previous Test tour of Sri Lanka in 2017, making his knowledge of local conditions unusually valuable to a squad otherwise light on recent experience there. The two-Test series marks an important early assessment of India's depth heading into a demanding season.

stories.title: A federal judge presses the Trump DOJ to explain why it's still withholding parts of the Epstein files
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, US District Judge **Emmet Sullivan** held a hearing pressing DOJ lawyers, led by Attorney General **Todd Blanche**, to explain why certain material remains redacted or withheld months after the transparency law took effect. The hearing stems from a lawsuit filed by an independent journalist alleging the DOJ's redactions and withholdings are unlawful; in **June**, Sullivan had already found some of the department's withholding violated the Act. Separately, another federal judge in New York, **Loretta Preska**, ruled this week that a batch of previously undisclosed Epstein-related documents can be made public, rejecting arguments from Epstein associate **Ghislaine Maxwell** that they should remain sealed.
key_points: A **federal judge** ordered DOJ officials to justify redactions in the Jeffrey Epstein files in court.
Attorney General **Todd Blanche** had to explain the department's refusal to unredact certain material.
The judge had already ruled in **June** that some withheld material violates the **Epstein Files Transparency Act**.
Withheld notes reportedly include material involving **allegations against President Trump**.
A separate ruling this week cleared other Epstein-related documents for release over Ghislaine Maxwell's objections.

depth.background: Congress passed the **Epstein Files Transparency Act** requiring the Justice Department to release investigative files related to the late financier and convicted sex offender **Jeffrey Epstein**, who died in 2019 while facing federal sex-trafficking charges. The law followed years of public pressure over what the government knew, and who else may have been implicated in Epstein's abuse network. Since the law passed, the DOJ has released millions of pages, but plaintiffs and journalists say officials have redacted or withheld material without adequate legal justification, including notes that reportedly reference the president.

stories.title: Bangladesh reach 96/1 at stumps, trailing Australia by just 102, after bowling the hosts out for 198
stories.what_happened: Australia were bowled out for just 198 on the opening day, with Hasan Mahmud claiming a career-best 6 for 55 — his third Test five-wicket haul — as Bangladesh's fast bowlers took all 10 Australian wickets, only the second time that has happened in the team's Test history. Steve Smith top-scored for the hosts with 71 off 109 balls. In reply, Bangladesh reached 96 for 1 by stumps, trailing by just 102 runs, with Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan both unbeaten and looking well set. Starc was the one Australian bowler who consistently troubled the Bangladesh batters, but the rest of the attack — including veteran spinner Nathan Lyon — couldn't find similar impact as conditions eased through the day.
key_points: Bangladesh closed day one at **96/1**, trailing Australia's first-innings **198** by just **102 runs**.
**Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan** both finished the day not out, building a solid platform in reply.
Only **Mitchell Starc** looked genuinely threatening with the ball; the rest of Australia's attack, including Nathan Lyon, made little impact.
Bangladesh had earlier bowled Australia out for **198**, with **Hasan Mahmud** taking a career-best **6 for 55**.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years** — and they've taken the early honours.

depth.background: Bangladesh arrived in Australia for their first Test tour of the country in 23 years, historically one of the toughest assignments in world cricket given Australia's pace-friendly home conditions. At Marrara Stadium in Darwin, Australia won the toss and chose to bat first — the conventional move at a ground where the pitch typically gets harder to bat on as a match wears on. Instead, Bangladesh's pace attack dismantled the Australian batting order on day one.

stories.title: India's Parliament passes 11 of 12 bills this Monsoon Session — with almost no debate and zero committee review
stories.what_happened: India's Parliament wrapped its 2026 Monsoon Session having introduced **12 Bills** and passed **11** of them, with only the Indian Statistical Institute Bill still pending. According to PRS Legislative Research, none of the 12 Bills introduced this session were referred to a Standing Committee for detailed scrutiny — a sharp drop from 2025, when five of 13 Bills went through that process. **Nine of the 11 passed Bills went through the Lok Sabha without a single MP other than the minister speaking on them.** The one exception was the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, which absorbed **17 hours 34 minutes** of debate across both Houses — more than the other ten Bills combined got (15 hours 24 minutes). Overall, the Lok Sabha sat for just **19%** of its scheduled functioning hours and the Rajya Sabha for **33%**, as repeated disruptions ate into the session. Two politically sensitive bills — on delimitation and FCRA reform — were shelved or sent to a Joint Parliamentary Committee rather than debated on the floor, with attention already shifting to 2027 state elections.
key_points: **11 of 12 Bills** introduced this Monsoon Session were passed — but **none** went to a Standing Committee for scrutiny.
**9 of 11** passed Bills saw **no MP besides the minister speak** on them before passing.
Lok Sabha functioned for just **19%** of its scheduled hours amid repeated disruptions.
One bill — on exam-cheating prevention — absorbed **more debate time than the other ten combined**.
Delimitation and a contentious FCRA bill were **shelved or deferred** as focus shifts to 2027 elections.

depth.background: India's Parliament holds three sessions a year, and the Standing Committee system — where a smaller cross-party group of MPs examines a bill clause-by-clause before it reaches the floor — exists specifically to catch drafting problems and unintended consequences that a rushed floor debate can miss. That system has been used less and less in recent years, and **PRS Legislative Research**, a respected nonpartisan tracker of Parliament's functioning, has flagged this session as a new low: **zero of 12 Bills** referred to committee, versus five of 13 last year. Sessions are frequently disrupted by opposition protests over unrelated political flashpoints, eating into the limited floor time available for actual legislative debate.

stories.title: Tankers are attacked and an oil spill spreads in the Strait of Hormuz, as Trump and Iran trade claims over who controls it
stories.what_happened: On Thursday evening, two tankers belonging to the UAE's state oil company ADNOC were attacked while transiting the Strait; no one was hurt and the vessels remained under control. Separately, the oil slick from the sunken Russian shadow-fleet tanker has now spread across an estimated **500 square miles**, threatening coastlines and shipping lanes. Commercial traffic through the Strait sank to just eight vessels tracked in the past week, a fraction of normal volumes. President Trump said the US has 'total control' over the Strait and suggested Washington 'might keep it', while Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned the US to 'be careful', calling Trump's claim 'fake intelligence'. Iran maintains the Strait is under its own military supervision and that no vessel can pass without its permission.
key_points: Two Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (**ADNOC**) tankers were attacked while transiting the Strait on **Thursday evening**; no injuries were reported.
An oil spill from a Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker that sank off Oman has now spread across roughly **500 square miles** of sea.
Traffic through the Strait has fallen to a one-week low of just **eight vessels**, versus dozens normally.
Trump claims the **US has 'total control'** of the Strait and might 'keep it'; Iran's foreign minister told him to 'be careful'.
Iran insists the waterway is under its **'complete management and control'** and that no ship can pass without its permission.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** normally passes through on its way from Gulf producers to global markets. Since a US-Iran conflict escalated this summer, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait and a sanctioned Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker — an aging, often uninsured ship used to move oil around Western sanctions — sank nearby, spilling crude. The US has responded by asserting it now effectively controls the waterway, a claim Tehran rejects.

thread.previously: We reported Iran was keeping the Strait effectively closed despite Trump's claims that it remained open, with tanker traffic already sinking to a one-week low.
thread.changed: Two ADNOC tankers were now directly attacked in the Strait, the Oman oil spill has grown to roughly 500 square miles, and Trump has escalated by claiming the US has 'total control' of the waterway — prompting a sharp warning from Iran's foreign minister.

prev_ref.title: Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is still shut despite Trump's claims, as tanker traffic sinks to a one-week low

stories.title: Israel says it won't leave southern Lebanon until Hezbollah disarms, walking back talk of indefinite occupation
stories.what_happened: On **August 12**, Israel's defense minister suggested Israeli forces could stay in southern Lebanon indefinitely, a comment that drew swift criticism from Washington for undercutting the framework deal it had brokered. A day later, on **August 13**, he qualified those remarks, saying Israel will withdraw — but only once Hezbollah is disarmed, not on a fixed timeline. Under the pilot program linked to the framework, Israeli forces are only slated to pull back from the zone between the **Yellow Line and the Litani River**, not from all of Israel's security positions in Lebanon. Lebanon's government, for its part, has struggled to convince or compel Hezbollah to hand over weapons it says it needs for deterrence.
key_points: Israel's defense minister said troops stay until Hezbollah is **fully disarmed**, walking back a remark a day earlier that had implied indefinite occupation
The retreat from those remarks came after **direct criticism from the US**, which brokered the underlying deal
A **June 26 framework agreement** ties any Israeli withdrawal to the Lebanese army removing Hezbollah's weapons
A pilot pullback covers only the strip between the **Yellow Line and the Litani River** — a partial, not full, withdrawal
Hezbollah, badly weakened in its 2024 war with Israel, has so far resisted giving up its arsenal

depth.background: Hezbollah is a heavily armed, Iran-backed political and militant movement based in Lebanon that has fought several wars with Israel since the 1980s. After a bruising 2024 conflict badly damaged Hezbollah's leadership and arsenal, the US brokered a **June 26, 2026 framework agreement**: Israeli troops would gradually leave southern Lebanon as the Lebanese national army verifiably disarmed Hezbollah and other non-state militias. Israel has occupied parts of southern Lebanon on and off for decades, arguing it needs a buffer zone to stop cross-border attacks. The disarmament process has moved slowly, leaving Israeli troops still present well past early informal deadlines.

stories.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak — already the country's worst ever — spreads to a sixth province after a traveler dies
stories.what_happened: Congolese health authorities confirmed the outbreak reached a **sixth province**, Bas-Uélé, after a motorcycle-taxi driver who had sought treatment at several hospitals died in the city of **Buta** on August 13, having traveled there from Isiro in neighboring Haut-Uélé province. His colleagues reportedly tried to forcibly take his body after his death, prompting a police intervention and raising fears more people may have been exposed before the case was identified. The DRC has recorded **4,665 confirmed cases and 2,184 deaths** as of the latest count, adding 99 new cases and 56 deaths in a single recent reporting period — making this **the largest Ebola outbreak in the country's history**, surpassing the previous record of 3,317 cases set in 2018-2020, and the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded anywhere. Over **600 patients** are currently hospitalized in isolation, and **54 of 151 health zones** across the six affected provinces are dealing with active transmission. Separately, neighboring Uganda declared its own related Ebola outbreak over on July 28.
key_points: The DRC has now confirmed **4,665 Ebola cases and 2,184 deaths**, making this the **worst Ebola outbreak in the country's history**, surpassing 2018-2020's 3,317 cases.
The outbreak reached a **sixth province, Bas-Uélé,** after a motorcycle-taxi driver traveled from another province and died in the city of **Buta**.
It's caused by the rarer **Bundibugyo strain** of Ebola — and neither licensed Ebola vaccine is proven to protect against it.
**54 of 151 health zones** across six provinces are now affected; over **600 patients** are currently hospitalized in isolation.
Police had to intervene after the dead man's colleagues tried to forcibly take his body — a reminder of how fear can undermine outbreak containment.

depth.background: Ebola is a severe, often fatal viral hemorrhagic fever first identified in the DRC in 1976, spread through contact with the bodily fluids of infected people or animals. This outbreak circulated quietly for **two to three months** before being officially declared in **May 2026**, and has since grown faster than any Ebola outbreak on record. It's caused by the **Bundibugyo virus**, a rarer relative of the Zaire ebolavirus that most vaccines and treatments were built for — a mismatch that leaves responders partly working blind. The two shots the world has stockpiled, **Ervebo** and the **Mvabea/Zabdeno** regimen, both target Zaire ebolavirus, and their protection against this strain is unproven.

stories.title: Hasan Mahmud's career-best 6-for stuns Australia as Bangladesh's pacers bowl them out for 198 in Darwin
stories.what_happened: Australia won the toss and chose to bat first at Marrara Stadium in Darwin, but were bowled out for 198 by the end of the first day. Hasan Mahmud led the destruction with a career-best 6 for 55 — his third Test five-wicket haul — while Taskin Ahmed and Ebadot Hossain chipped in with two wickets each. It marked only the second time in Bangladesh's Test history that fast bowlers have taken all 10 wickets in an innings, after a similar feat in Rawalpindi in 2024. Steven Smith was the one bright spot for Australia, top-scoring with 71 off 109 balls including seven fours and a six.
key_points: Bangladesh bowled Australia out for just **198** on day one of the first Test in Darwin.
**Hasan Mahmud** took a career-best **6 for 55** — his third Test five-wicket haul.
Bangladesh's **fast bowlers took all 10 Australian wickets** — only the second time that's happened in the team's Test history.
**Steven Smith** top-scored for Australia with **71 off 109 balls**.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.

depth.background: Bangladesh has not played a Test series in Australia in 23 years, making this tour a rare and significant assignment for a team more often associated with home conditions and spin bowling than fast bowling on the road. The first Test began August 13 at Marrara Stadium in Darwin and runs through August 17.

stories.title: Cadillac F1 co-owner Mark Walter sells the LA Lakers for a record $12.5 billion — but keeps his F1 stake
stories.what_happened: Walter has agreed to sell the Lakers to **Bob Iger**, the former Disney chief executive, and **Josh Kushner**, a businessman and investor, for a **record $12.5 billion** — a roughly 25% gain on the $10 billion he paid just **10 months earlier**. In a joint statement, Kushner and Iger said they were 'deeply honoured' to become 'stewards' of the franchise. Notably, Walter is **not** selling his stake in Cadillac's Formula 1 team, which he co-owns alongside TWG — this transaction covers the Lakers only. The sale's timing has drawn attention because Walter has been under investigation by federal prosecutors and the SEC over roughly **$16 billion** in potential financial improprieties and tax fraud.
key_points: **Mark Walter** sold the Los Angeles Lakers for a record **$12.5 billion**.
The buyers are former Disney CEO **Bob Iger** and businessman **Josh Kushner**.
Walter bought the team for **$10 billion just 10 months ago**, in October 2025.
He **retains his ownership stake in Cadillac's F1 team**, which he co-owns with TWG — only the Lakers were sold.
The sale's timing coincides with a **federal and SEC investigation** into roughly $16 billion in alleged financial improprieties tied to Walter.

depth.background: **Mark Walter** is the CEO of investment firm Guggenheim Partners and, through his TWG Global holding company, co-owns Formula 1's **Cadillac** team — the newest entrant on the 2026 grid. He bought the **Los Angeles Lakers** NBA franchise from the Buss family for a $10 billion valuation in October 2025. Walter and TWG have also faced scrutiny from federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over alleged financial irregularities.

stories.title: Israeli settlers besiege Palestinian homes in the West Bank for five nights, drawing a US rebuke of 'terror'
stories.what_happened: For **five consecutive nights**, dozens of Israeli settlers encircled three Palestinian homes on the edge of Qusra, pitching tents outside and cutting off the residents' water and electricity, forcing families to drink from a well as supplies ran low. Israeli troops eventually moved in and said they dismantled **two illegal outposts** near the town, detaining one Israeli settler, but were met by more settlers who rolled boulders into the road and threw rocks; soldiers responded with sound grenades and pepper spray before pulling back. **US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee** — normally a strong defender of Israel's government — broke with that pattern and called the siege a **'horrific act of terror.'** In the aftermath, a mosque in Qusra was set on fire and the Hebrew word for **'revenge'** was found spray-painted on its wall, according to CNN and the Washington Post.
key_points: Israeli settlers surrounded **three Palestinian homes** near Qusra for **five straight nights**, cutting water and power.
The **US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee**, called the siege a **'horrific act of terror.'**
Israeli troops dismantled **two illegal outposts** but were pelted with rocks by settlers who kept arriving.
The **UN** says Qusra saw **more settler attacks than any other West Bank community** in 2026.
A mosque in Qusra was set on fire, with **'revenge'** spray-painted on its wall in Hebrew.

depth.background: The West Bank is Palestinian territory that Israel has occupied since 1967; roughly 500,000 Israeli settlers now live there in communities most of the world considers illegal under international law, alongside about 3 million Palestinians. Settler violence against Palestinian villages has been rising for years, often carried out by small groups who set up unauthorized outposts and try to force Palestinian families off land they've lived on for generations. **Qusra**, a town of a few thousand people, has become one of the worst-hit places, recording more settler attacks than anywhere else in the West Bank this year according to the UN. Israel's military is legally responsible for protecting Palestinian civilians there, which is why the length of this siege — and the slow response — drew such sharp international criticism.

stories.title: Taiwan deliberately slowed mobile internet for 16 million people to rehearse for a Chinese invasion
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, Taiwanese telecom operators throttled mobile internet speeds down to **256 Kbps** — slow enough that only basic texting works, not video or most apps — across seven northern jurisdictions including Taipei, New Taipei City, and Keelung, from 2:30 to 3:00pm local time. This was the second of two throttling phases run as part of **Han Kuang 42**, Taiwan's largest annual military exercise, which ran from August 5 to 14 this year. Combined, the two throttling phases affected roughly **16 million people**, about 70% of Taiwan's total population. The **Taiwan Stock Exchange** was granted an exemption so trading wasn't disrupted. President **Lai Ching-te** publicly apologized for the inconvenience, telling residents 'we ask for your understanding and support, as this is a necessary drill.' The exercise is explicitly designed to model how the island would cope if China attempted an invasion or blockade and tried to cut off communications.
key_points: Telecom carriers throttled mobile data to **256 Kbps** — barely enough for text messages — across two rounds covering **~16 million people**, about **70% of Taiwan's population**.
The second throttle hit **seven jurisdictions in northern Taiwan**, including Taipei, from 2:30-3:00pm local time on Thursday.
It's the final phase of **Han Kuang 42**, Taiwan's largest annual military exercise, which ran August 5-14.
President **Lai Ching-te** personally apologized for the inconvenience, calling it a 'necessary drill.'
The goal: test whether civilians and businesses can still function if China knocks out or jams normal telecom networks during an invasion or blockade.

depth.background: **Han Kuang** is Taiwan's flagship annual exercise simulating a Chinese invasion, and it has grown more elaborate each year as tensions with **Beijing** have escalated — China claims Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out taking it by force. Past editions focused mostly on military maneuvers; this year added a large-scale **civilian resilience** component, testing whether ordinary people, hospitals, and businesses could keep functioning if China's real war plan includes disabling or jamming Taiwan's communications networks, a tactic seen in other modern conflicts. The drill deliberately picked telecom infrastructure because a full communications blackout is considered one of the most disruptive opening moves an attacker could make.

stories.title: Canada and the US race to strike a trade deal before Washington's Aug. 19 deadline for 50% tariffs
stories.what_happened: Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief negotiator Janice Charette met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Thursday, Aug. 13 — their second sit-down with Greer this week, part of a run of meetings that has kept them in Washington since Monday. The talks are racing against an **Aug. 19 deadline**, after which the US is set to impose **50% tariffs** on about **$20 billion** worth of Canadian exports, covering goods like alcohol, hockey sticks, and cement. Crucially, these tariffs would carry no exemption for goods that already comply with CUSMA — unlike most of Trump's other tariff actions. Greer has said the tariffs respond to three things: provincial bans on US liquor, Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US vehicles and parts, and Canada's dairy quota system, which Washington says treats US dairy worse than the EU gets under a separate deal. Canadian officials are reportedly prepared to lift the alcohol bans and offer concessions on autos and dairy in exchange for tariff relief, hoping to have a deal framework ready to show Trump before next Wednesday. PM Mark Carney has called the talks "constructive" but says Canada "will not accept a bad deal," keeping retaliation on the table if talks collapse.
key_points: Canada's trade minister met the US Trade Representative in Washington for the **second time this week**, six days before a hard deadline.
Without a deal, the US will impose **50% tariffs** on roughly **$20 billion** of Canadian exports — including alcohol, hockey sticks, and cement — starting **Aug. 19**.
Unlike most other Trump tariffs, these come with **no exemption** for goods that comply with the existing US-Canada-Mexico trade agreement (CUSMA).
Washington's three complaints: **provincial bans on US alcohol**, Canada's retaliatory **auto tariffs**, and its **dairy quota system**.
Canada is reportedly ready to **drop the alcohol bans** and ease auto/dairy barriers for relief, though PM Mark Carney says he **won't accept a bad deal**.

depth.background: Trump has used tariff threats repeatedly this year as leverage in trade disputes, and Canada has been a repeated target despite the two countries' deep trade ties and the existing free-trade deal, **CUSMA** (the Canada-US-Mexico Agreement, the successor to NAFTA). Most Canadian provinces — every one except Alberta and Saskatchewan — pulled American alcohol from liquor-store shelves earlier this year in retaliation for previous Trump tariffs, which the US now cites as a grievance. Canada, in turn, has its own retaliatory tariffs on US-made vehicles and parts, and a dairy quota system that limits US dairy access — both now also on Washington's complaint list.

stories.title: Pakistan's pacers claim six wickets but their top order is left chasing 305 in an England warm-up match at Beckenham
stories.what_happened: In their three-day warm-up fixture at Beckenham against a Professional County Club Select XI, Pakistan's bowling attack — led by **Ali and Abbas, who shared six wickets** — bowled the Select XI out for 305. Pakistan's own batting effort in reply was slow to get going: they finished the first day on **44 for 0 after 13 overs**, still 261 runs behind. The match continues through August 15, giving Pakistan's top order more time at the crease to find rhythm before the series proper begins. The tour's first Test starts August 19 at Headingley in Leeds, followed by matches at Lord's and Edgbaston.
key_points: A **Professional County Club Select XI scored 305** against Pakistan's bowlers in a three-day warm-up match at Beckenham.
Pakistan bowlers **Ali and Abbas shared six wickets** between them to restrict the Select XI's total.
In reply, Pakistan closed Day 1 on just **44/0 after 13 overs**, still trailing by 261 runs.
The match is Pakistan's final tune-up before the **first Test against England begins August 19 at Headingley, Leeds**.
Pakistan's Test squad is captained by **Babar Azam**, on tour after a series in the West Indies.

depth.background: Pakistan's tour of England is part of the **ICC World Test Championship 2025–27 cycle**, and comes directly after a Test series in the West Indies, meaning the squad has had limited turnaround time between assignments. Warm-up matches like this one against a County Select XI are the last chance for touring teams to adjust to English conditions — different pitch and weather behaviour from anywhere else in the world — before a Test series begins. Pakistan's squad, led by Babar Azam, arrived in England having also brought in a new batting coach, Michael Smith, ahead of this series.

stories.title: The FIA quietly lifts its post-Ukraine-war ban on Russian and Belarusian drivers, without explaining why
stories.what_happened: The FIA's **World Motor Sport Council** — its top decision-making body — voted on **August 3, 2026** to lift the restrictions, and the decision was formally circulated to national federations, teams and officials on **August 13**. Under the new rules, Russian and Belarusian competitors, national teams and officials can take part in international events **without restriction**, and are free to display their **flags, colours and anthems** again. The requirement to sign a neutrality commitment has been scrapped. One restriction remains: **no international event can be held inside Russia or Belarus** "until further notice." The FIA gave **no public explanation** for the timing or reasoning behind the reversal, which several outlets noted was unusual given how detailed the original 2022 ban's justification had been.
key_points: FIA's World Motor Sport Council decided on **August 3** to lift restrictions, confirmed in a circular sent **August 13**
Russian and Belarusian drivers, teams and officials can now compete under their **own flags and anthems**
The mandatory **neutrality pledge** signed since 2022 no longer applies
Competitions still **cannot be held inside Russia or Belarus** itself
No public explanation was given for the reversal, four years after the war in Ukraine triggered the ban

depth.background: In March 2022, weeks after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the FIA — motorsport's global governing body — barred Russian and Belarusian competitors from racing under their national colours anywhere in the world, mirroring bans imposed by the IOC and other sports bodies. Drivers were only allowed to compete as neutral athletes, without flags, anthems or national identification, and had to sign a declaration condemning the war to be cleared to race. The measure affected everyone from junior karting racers to any Russian nationals hoping to reach Formula 1. The FIA has not previously wavered from the ban despite periodic lobbying from Russian motorsport federations.

stories.title: Cadillac's F1 team fires its own boss a week before the season resumes, hands the wheel to a former Alpine chief
stories.what_happened: Formula 1 newcomer **Cadillac** has fired **Graeme Lowdon**, the team boss who built its debut season, and replaced him with **Marcin Budkowski**, a former **Alpine/Renault executive director**, just a week before the season resumes at Zandvoort. Team CEO **Dan Towriss** confirmed the call was his alone — 'It was my decision. It wasn't a mutual decision' — and said Lowdon was only informed on Wednesday morning. Towriss said the switch was not a reaction to Cadillac's on-track struggles (the team has yet to score a single point, with a best finish of 13th) but a deliberate shift from the team's 'build phase' into its next stage. Budkowski has deep F1 technical pedigree: he worked at **Ferrari** (2002–2007) and **McLaren** (2007–2014, rising to Head of Aerodynamics), then spent three years as the FIA's top technical official overseeing the sport's rules, before joining Renault/Alpine as executive/technical director. His task now is to give Cadillac a longer-term competitiveness plan rather than firefight the current car.
key_points: Cadillac **fired team boss Graeme Lowdon** just a week before the season resumes at Zandvoort.
Replacement **Marcin Budkowski** previously worked at **Ferrari, McLaren, the FIA, and Alpine/Renault**.
CEO Dan Towriss says the call was **his alone** — Lowdon found out only on **Wednesday morning**.
Cadillac has **yet to score a point** in its debut F1 season, with a best finish of 13th.
Towriss insists the change is about a **longer-term vision**, not a panic reaction to results.

depth.background: Cadillac is Formula 1's newest team, entering the grid in 2026 as the sport's 11th constructor after years of General Motors pushing for entry. Graeme Lowdon, a respected paddock veteran who previously ran the Manor/Virgin F1 team, was hired to lead Cadillac through its build-up and debut season. Marcin Budkowski is a well-known technical figure in the paddock — he once ran F1's own technical department for the FIA, the sport's governing body, before crossing over to run Alpine's technical operations, giving him rare insight into both the regulator's side and a rival constructor's side of the sport.

stories.title: Red Bull reportedly lines up Aston Martin's Tom McCullough to replace Lambiase
stories.what_happened: German media reported this week that Red Bull has all but finalized a deal to hire **Tom McCullough** away from Aston Martin, where he has spent **13 years**, most recently as **Performance Director**. At Red Bull, McCullough would take the role of **Head of Racing**, overseeing all trackside operations and managing the race engineers during Grand Prix weekends — effectively succeeding **Gianpiero Lambiase**, who has been Max Verstappen's dedicated race engineer for years. McCullough is expected to leave Aston Martin at the **end of the 2026 season**. Neither Red Bull nor McCullough has officially confirmed the move, and outlets are treating it as a strong, well-sourced report rather than a done deal.
key_points: Red Bull is reported to have agreed to bring in Aston Martin's **Tom McCullough** as its new **Head of Racing**, per German media.
He would replace **Gianpiero Lambiase**, long known as **Max Verstappen's race engineer** and a senior figure at Red Bull.
McCullough has been Aston Martin's **Performance Director for 13 years** and would leave the team at the **end of 2026**.
The move is **unconfirmed by both teams** — it's reported, not officially announced.
It's the latest in a string of **personnel moves** as Red Bull rebuilds its technical structure, following reported arrivals from Mercedes.

depth.background: Formula 1 teams compete as much on **engineering talent** as on cars — senior race engineers and performance directors move between rival teams for big raises just like drivers do, and these moves can meaningfully shift a team's competitiveness over a season or two. **Red Bull** has had a turbulent 2026 season on-track and has been rebuilding key parts of its technical and trackside leadership. **Aston Martin**, meanwhile, has invested heavily in facilities and personnel in recent years under new ownership, aiming to become a genuine front-running team.

stories.title: UN satellite survey: Gaza building destruction has grown nearly 10% since the ceasefire took effect
stories.what_happened: UNOSAT's latest satellite-based assessment estimates the number of destroyed structures across Gaza has increased by about **9%** since the ceasefire declaration, even though large-scale fighting has stopped. Roughly **82% of Gaza's buildings — about 200,000 structures** — are now damaged, with two-thirds of those fully destroyed. UNRWA says it has received reports, which it could not independently verify due to access restrictions, of demolitions hitting schools and other UN facilities in Israeli-controlled areas. UN agencies say the destruction, combined with continued access limits, is choking humanitarian movement and complicating aid delivery.
key_points: A new **UN Satellite Centre (UNOSAT)** assessment finds destroyed structures in Gaza rose by nearly **9-10%** since the October 2025 ceasefire began.
About **82% of all structures in Gaza — roughly 200,000 buildings** — are now damaged or destroyed.
**UNRWA** says it has received unverified reports of demolitions affecting schools and UN facilities in areas under Israeli military control.
Access restrictions mean the UN **cannot independently verify** many of these newer demolition reports.

depth.background: Gaza's ceasefire, part of US President Trump's peace plan, took effect in **October 2025** after roughly two years of war that displaced more than **one million people** and reduced entire neighborhoods to rubble. Israel's military currently controls close to **70% of Gaza's territory** under the ceasefire's terms, with lines of control that aid groups say keep shifting. The ceasefire silenced most large-scale combat but did not end all incidents on the ground.

stories.title: Supreme Court slams Karnataka's 'absurd' terror-trial delays, orders a dedicated fast-track court
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court bench, hearing a bail plea from Shahid Khan — in custody since **September 22, 2022** in a case involving PFI members — pulled up the Karnataka government over what it called an 'absurd' prosecution plan. The state's case involves 707 witnesses in total, but its own submission proposed examining only 50 of them specifically in relation to Khan, with no clear timeline for finishing the trial. The bench said the state cannot have "the luxury of prolonging trial for years" while a citizen sits in jail awaiting trial, calling it "callousness" for a prosecuting agency to withhold a clear picture of when a case will conclude. As a remedy, the Court directed the Karnataka government to set up an **additional special court** to hear UAPA cases exclusively, on a day-to-day basis, with the necessary approvals to be granted within two weeks.
key_points: The Supreme Court criticized Karnataka's prosecution plan in a **UAPA (terror law) case** as 'absurd'
The accused, Shahid Khan, has been in custody since **September 2022** without trial completing
Of **707 witnesses** in the case, the state proposed examining just 50 in relation to Khan — with no timeline
The Court called it **'callousness'** for the state to keep a citizen jailed without a clear trial plan
It ordered Karnataka to set up an **additional special court** dedicated to UAPA cases within two weeks

depth.background: The UAPA (Unlawful Activities Prevention Act) is India's main anti-terror law, allowing extended pre-trial detention and making bail much harder to get than under ordinary criminal law. Critics have long argued it lets the state keep people in jail for years without ever proving a case in court, effectively making the process itself the punishment. This case involves an accused linked to the **Popular Front of India (PFI)**, an Islamic organisation the government banned in 2022 over alleged extremist links, and the ruling was delivered by a bench led by Chief Justice of India **Surya Kant**.

stories.title: Sensex snaps its losing streak to close 114 points higher, but Nifty falls for a third straight day
stories.what_happened: Indian markets closed mixed today: the **Sensex gained 113.61 points (0.15%)** to end at **78,079.96**, breaking a two-session losing run, while the **Nifty 50 slipped 40.10 points (0.16%)** to **24,395.85** — its third consecutive down day. Within the Nifty, the metal index fell **1.05%**, and private banks and oil & gas names also weighed on the index, while **FMCG, IT, and media stocks** advanced and helped the Sensex hold onto gains. The divergence between the two indices reflects how narrow, large-cap-weighted gains — which lift the Sensex — can mask broader weakness spread across more sectors, which the Nifty's wider base picks up. Traders pointed to the **cooler-than-expected India and US inflation readings** released this week as the main source of support, since both raise hopes that central banks can hold interest rates steady rather than needing to hike further.
key_points: The **Sensex** rose **113.61 points (+0.15%)** to close at **78,079.96**, snapping a two-day losing streak.
The **Nifty 50** fell **40.10 points (-0.16%)** to **24,395.85**, extending its own losing streak to a **third day**.
**Metal, private-bank, and oil & gas stocks** dragged the index down, while **FMCG, IT, and media** shares gained.
Softer-than-expected **India and US inflation** data kept hopes alive that the RBI and the Fed can hold a patient, steady policy stance.

depth.background: India's two benchmark indices — the **Sensex** (30 large companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange) and the **Nifty 50** (50 large companies on the National Stock Exchange) — had been sliding for the past two trading days, pressured by the Tata Group leadership shake-up, a weak rupee, and elevated oil prices tied to the Strait of Hormuz standoff. This morning's indicators had pointed to a stronger session after **July's US inflation print came in cooler than expected**, easing worries about how aggressively the Fed needs to keep interest rates high.

stories.title: Scotland and Canada clash again in Dundee with 2027 World Cup qualification hopes on the line
stories.what_happened: Playing at their home ground of Forthill in Dundee, **Scotland batted first** against Canada in the 126th match of the League 2 cycle. At the time of writing, Scotland had reached **267/4**, with batter Michael Jones unbeaten on 41 and wicketkeeper Matthew Cross also not out, building a total aimed at extending their strong position near the top of the table. Scotland currently sit second in the League 2 standings with 38 points from 32 matches (16 wins), while Canada are fifth with 20 points from 20 games and need a strong finish to stay in contention for a World Cup Qualifier spot.
key_points: Scotland and Canada are playing their second meeting in a week in the **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2**, this time in Dundee
Scotland sit **2nd** in the League 2 table with 38 points from 32 matches; Canada are **5th** with 20 points from 20 games
The two teams last met on **August 7**, when Scotland won by 9 runs in a high-scoring game (281/7 vs 272)
League 2 results feed directly into qualification for the **2027 Cricket World Cup** — making every match here count for both sides
Scotland reached **267/4** in their innings today, with Michael Jones unbeaten on 41, as they push to extend their points lead

depth.background: The **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2** is a multi-year one-day international league for cricket's second tier of nations, running from 2023 to 2027. It's a key step on the qualification pathway toward the **2027 Cricket World Cup**, so results here have real stakes even though the teams involved — Scotland, Canada, Namibia, UAE, USA, and others — rarely make global headlines. Scotland and Canada have faced each other repeatedly in this cycle, most recently on August 7 in a tight 9-run Scotland win, and today's rematch in Dundee is part of the same tightly-fought race for qualification points.

stories.title: India readies its 80th Independence Day, reviving 'Vande Mataram' at the Red Fort for the first time in 150 years
stories.what_happened: The Indian government has finalized plans for the **80th Independence Day** ceremony on August 15, with the theme **'Yuva Shakti for Viksit Bharat@2047'**. For the first time, **'Vande Mataram'** will be sung from the Red Fort ramparts as part of the official proceedings, marking **150 years** since the song was composed. Around **2,500 National Cadet Corps (NCC) cadets and My Bharat volunteers** will physically form the words 'Vande Mataram' at Gyanpath near the fort, while an **Indian Air Force Mi-17 helicopter** carrying a commemorative banner will shower flower petals over the gathering. The government has also organized military band performances at **343 locations nationwide** between August 8–15, and the PM's speech will be translated live into more than **22 Indian languages** using the government's **Bhashini** AI translation system.
key_points: India marks its **80th Independence Day** on August 15, themed **'Yuva Shakti for Viksit Bharat@2047'**.
2026 marks **150 years of Vande Mataram**, sung from the Red Fort ramparts for the first time in the ceremony's history.
Around **2,500 NCC cadets and My Bharat volunteers** will form the words 'Vande Mataram' at Gyanpath.
An Indian Air Force **Mi-17 helicopter** will shower flower petals while carrying a commemorative banner.
**Bhashini**, India's AI translation system, will render the PM's speech live in over **22 Indian languages**.

depth.background: India's Independence Day, marking the country's freedom from British colonial rule in **1947**, is celebrated every August 15 with a flag-hoisting and prime ministerial address from the ramparts of the **Red Fort** in Delhi. Each year's ceremony carries a theme reflecting the government's political messaging; this year's focus on **'Yuva Shakti' (youth power)** ties into the government's **Viksit Bharat@2047** vision — a goal of making India a fully developed economy by the 100th anniversary of independence in 2047. **'Vande Mataram'** ('I bow to thee, Mother') is a patriotic song written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay that played a major role in India's freedom movement and was adopted as the national song in 1950; 2026 marks 150 years since it was first composed.

thread.previously: Yesterday's brief noted Delhi had locked down central roads for Independence Day's full-dress rehearsal, with facial-recognition CCTV and a drone ban in force.
thread.changed: The government has now detailed the ceremony itself: the first-ever singing of 'Vande Mataram' from the Red Fort ramparts, a 2,500-strong human formation, and AI-translated broadcast of the PM's speech.
