stories.title: US senators demand answers after sailors try to jump off the USS Abraham Lincoln during a record-length deployment
stories.what_happened: Sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have now been at sea for **more than 260 days**, with **over 200 days** since the ship's last port call — believed to be the longest stretch without shore leave for a US carrier in the modern era. Family members and unnamed crew have told reporters that multiple sailors have either attempted to go overboard or been physically restrained before they could. One family described a sailor texting that '**he hopes he doesn't wake up tomorrow**.' The ship was originally meant to return home months ago but was instead extended and redirected toward the Middle East as part of the US military posture around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. Democratic senators Ruben Gallego and Richard Blumenthal are now demanding the Navy grant Congress an oversight visit and provide a full accounting of overboard and self-harm incidents by **August 27**. The Navy has so far declined to confirm exact numbers, and it's unclear when the strike group will finally return to port.
key_points: The **USS Abraham Lincoln** carrier strike group has been at sea for **more than 260 days**, without a single port call in over **200 days** — a modern-day record.
Multiple sailors have reportedly tried to **jump overboard**, with families describing crew texting that they 'hope they don't wake up tomorrow.'
The ship, carrying roughly **5,000 sailors and Marines**, was diverted from a routine Pacific deployment to the Middle East for Iran-related operations.
Democratic senators **Ruben Gallego and Richard Blumenthal** are demanding a congressional oversight visit and Navy answers by **August 27**.
The Navy has not confirmed how many overboard or self-harm incidents have actually occurred.

depth.background: The USS Abraham Lincoln and its strike group left San Diego on **November 21, 2025**, on what was originally billed as a standard Pacific deployment. As tensions over the **Strait of Hormuz** and Iran escalated through 2026, the Navy redirected the carrier to the Middle East instead of bringing it home. US Navy deployments are typically capped around six to seven months precisely because extended time at sea erodes crew welfare — mental health, family strain, and morale all suffer the longer a ship stays out. This deployment has now blown past that norm by months, with no announced return date.

stories.title: A data center operator is exploring a $100 billion IPO — a sign of how big the AI building boom has gotten
stories.what_happened: According to people familiar with the matter, **Vantage Data Centers** has held preliminary discussions in recent weeks about possible exit paths for its private-equity owners, meeting informally with financial advisers about a stock market listing or a sale. An **IPO** could value the company at around **$100 billion** and raise roughly **$10 billion** for the business — a figure that would make it the largest-ever data center IPO. The company is also weighing a sale, including selling a stake to new investors, as an alternative route. Any deal remains at an early, non-binding stage, and could happen as soon as next year if it proceeds. The exploration comes as AI-driven demand for computing power keeps pushing valuations for data-center operators sharply higher.
key_points: **Vantage Data Centers** is exploring an IPO that could value it at roughly **$100 billion**, which would make it the largest data-center listing ever
The company, backed by private equity firm **Silver Lake** and infrastructure investor **DigitalBridge**, could raise around **$10 billion** in the offering
A **sale**, including a partial stake sale, is also being considered as an alternative to going public
Talks are still preliminary — no formal process has launched, and timing, size, and structure could all change
Vantage has already raised roughly **$11 billion** since late 2023 to build out data centers, underscoring how much capital the AI infrastructure race is consuming

depth.background: **Data centers** are the physical warehouses full of servers and specialized chips (like Nvidia's GPUs) that actually run AI models — every ChatGPT-style answer or AI image is computed inside one. As AI demand has exploded, so has the need for these facilities, and the private equity and infrastructure firms that own them have been pouring in tens of billions of dollars to build bigger ones, faster. Vantage Data Centers is one of the largest such operators globally, and its owners — Silver Lake and DigitalBridge — have already put in over **$9 billion** in equity since 2023 to fund its expansion.

stories.title: A sanctioned Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker sinking off Oman has spread oil across roughly 800 square kilometers of protected coastline
stories.what_happened: Oman's Environment Authority confirmed this week that oil leaking from the grounded, partly-submerged Caroline Bezengi has now reached the country's mainland beaches, around **Ras Madrakah**, some 200 km north of the islands where the tanker first ran into trouble. The slick has expanded dramatically — from roughly **45 square kilometers** on July 26 to about **800 square kilometers** by August 7, according to satellite tracking cited by the Associated Press — with up to **40 km of coastline** now affected. The tanker was carrying close to **one million barrels** of Russian crude when the explosion happened in June, and monsoon-season winds and currents have been pushing the spill further and faster than initially expected.
key_points: The **Caroline Bezengi**, a sanctioned tanker in Russia's "shadow fleet," is sinking after an unexplained explosion in **June**.
It was carrying almost **1 million barrels** of Russian crude bound for Asia when it first reported trouble.
The slick has grown from about **45 sq km** in late July to roughly **800 sq km** by early August, and has now reached Oman's mainland coast.
It threatens the **Hallaniyat Islands** nature reserve, home to nesting sea turtles and the rare **Arabian Sea humpback whale**.
No country or group has claimed responsibility for the **explosion** that crippled the ship, and no party has yet accepted cleanup liability.

depth.background: Since Western sanctions hit Russian oil exports over the Ukraine war, a "shadow fleet" of aging, opaquely-owned tankers has grown up to keep that oil moving — dodging mainstream insurers and price-cap rules by operating outside normal maritime oversight. The **Caroline Bezengi**, a 274-metre tanker identified as part of that fleet, first reported an explosion onboard on **June 8** off Yemen and has been slowly sinking ever since near **Al Qibliyah Island** in Oman's **Hallaniyat Islands** — a protected marine reserve. Because shadow-fleet ships are deliberately hard to trace to a responsible owner or insurer, incidents like this one are difficult to hold anyone accountable for.

stories.title: Leclerc and Gasly wipe their FIA penalty points clean heading into Zandvoort
stories.what_happened: Charles Leclerc entered the resumption of the season with a **clean super licence** after a penalty point from the **2025 Hungarian Grand Prix** — issued for erratic driving while defending his position from George Russell — passed its 12-month expiry. Pierre Gasly's **two penalty points**, handed down for causing a collision with Carlos Sainz at the same race, had already expired on **August 3**. Neither driver currently carries any points on the FIA's rolling ledger, removing any risk of an automatic ban heading into the run-in.
key_points: **Charles Leclerc's** penalty point from the 2025 Hungarian Grand Prix has expired, taking him back to **zero points** on his super licence.
**Pierre Gasly's** two penalty points from a collision with Carlos Sainz at the same race expired on **August 3**.
Under F1 rules, a driver hits **12 penalty points within 12 months** and gets an automatic **one-race ban**.
Leclerc's point had been given for driving erratically while defending against George Russell.
Both drivers head into the resumed season at **Zandvoort** with a clean licence.

depth.background: The FIA's penalty-point system tracks driving infractions on a rolling 12-month basis: points are added for offenses like causing a collision or driving unsafely, and a driver who accumulates 12 or more within that window is automatically banned for one race. Points expire exactly a year after they're issued, so as races from summer 2025 roll off the 12-month window, several drivers are quietly clearing their slate heading into the second half of the 2026 season.

stories.title: Rain threatens to soak every session of F1's final-ever Dutch Grand Prix
stories.what_happened: New weather forecasts for the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, running **August 21-23** at Zandvoort, show a particularly high chance of rain across all three days of track action — practice, the Saturday sprint race, and Sunday's main Grand Prix. It's the first round back after F1's summer break, and it's being promoted as the **last-ever Dutch Grand Prix** at this point in the calendar, which raises the stakes for what could already be a chaotic, rain-affected send-off. Zandvoort's signature steeply banked corners, like the 18-degree 'Hugenholtz' hairpin, become significantly more challenging and prone to accidents when wet. Weekend tickets are already sold out, meaning a rain-soaked weekend would play out in front of a full house.
key_points: Weather forecasts show a **high chance of rain across all three days**, including the sprint race, at Zandvoort.
This is set to be the **last-ever Dutch Grand Prix** at the current calendar slot, adding extra stakes to the weekend.
The 2026 Dutch GP runs **August 21-23**, F1's first race back after the summer break.
Zandvoort's banked corners, including the steep **Turn 3 'Hugenholtz'**, get significantly trickier to drive in the wet.
Weekend tickets for the race are already **sold out**, so a washout would disappoint a packed crowd.

depth.background: The Dutch Grand Prix returned to F1's calendar in 2021 after a 35-year absence, driven largely by the popularity of home favorite Max Verstappen, and quickly became one of the most electric atmospheres on the calendar thanks to its passionate orange-clad crowds at the seaside Zandvoort circuit. The track is known for its unusually steep, banked corners — a layout borrowed from oval racing — which makes it especially demanding when conditions are wet and grip is reduced. This edition is being billed as the **final running of the race**, adding sentimental weight on top of the usual championship stakes.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll rises to 273 as rescuers enter a 'final phase' — but the missing count drops sharply as thousands are found
stories.what_happened: Colombia's disaster-management agency says the confirmed death toll has climbed to **273**, with 3,824 injured, as of the latest count. Crucially, the number of people still classified as missing has fallen dramatically — from more than 2,700 reported missing earlier in the week to **377** now — as search teams worked through the rubble and located thousands of previously unaccounted-for residents. One notable rescue: a 32-year-old woman was pulled out alive in Pereira after more than 36 hours trapped. Authorities say rescue operations have now entered their 'final phase', with international help including roughly 40 US search-and-rescue personnel. The quake damaged over 200 roads, five airports, and 44 water systems (aqueducts) across the affected region.
key_points: The death toll from Colombia's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has risen to **273**, with **3,824** people reported injured.
The number still listed as missing has fallen sharply to **377**, down from over 2,700 reported missing days earlier, as many were located.
A **32-year-old woman was pulled alive** from rubble in Pereira after being trapped for more than **36 hours**.
Rescue operations have entered a **'final phase'**, with US urban search-and-rescue teams (~40 people) helping local first responders.
More than **200 roads**, 5 airports, and 44 aqueducts were damaged, hitting the hard-hit Pereira and Cali regions.

depth.background: A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on **August 10**, centered near San José del Palmar in Chocó department — the country's strongest quake in a century. It flattened buildings and infrastructure across the Pereira and Cali regions, triggering a mass rescue operation. Colombia's new government faced criticism over aid access and the pace of the response in the disaster's first days.

thread.previously: We reported the death toll had passed 265 with over 2,700 people still reported missing, as rescue teams struggled to reach the earthquake's epicenter.
thread.changed: The death toll has risen only modestly to 273, but the missing count has collapsed to 377 as thousands were located — and officials now say rescue operations are entering their 'final phase'.

stories.title: Australia win the toss and bat first as the historic Bangladesh Test begins in Darwin
stories.what_happened: Australia won the toss and captain **Pat Cummins** elected to bat first on a green Darwin surface in humid conditions, with opener **Travis Head** expecting a tough opening period against the new ball. Australia's confirmed XI is: Jake Weatherald, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins (captain), Nathan Lyon, and Josh Hazlewood. Both Green and Webster won selection battles for their all-rounder spots, and Lyon returns to the side after sitting out the back end of the Ashes with a hamstring injury. This marks the first time in over a year that Australia's leading pace trio — Cummins, Hazlewood, and Starc — has played together. Bangladesh has named Ebadot Hossain and Mahmudul Hasan in its own XI as the tourists begin their first Test series on Australian soil in 23 years.
key_points: Australia captain **Pat Cummins won the toss** and chose to **bat first** on a green, humid Darwin pitch.
The confirmed Australia XI includes **Cameron Green and Beau Webster**, both winning selection battles for the spot.
**Nathan Lyon returns** after missing the back end of the Ashes with a hamstring injury.
The Cummins-Hazlewood-Starc pace trio is playing together for the **first time in more than a year**.
This is Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**, marking a historic return fixture.

depth.background: Bangladesh last toured Australia for a Test series back in 2003, when Australia won comfortably — so this five-day match at Darwin's Marrara Cricket Ground, starting the current series, is being treated as a genuinely historic fixture for Bangladeshi cricket. Australia has been juggling injuries and form questions in its bowling attack over the past year, including during the recent Ashes series, which is why the reunion of its three most experienced fast bowlers together is being watched closely.

thread.previously: We reported Australia was set to reunite its Cummins-Starc-Hazlewood pace attack for the first Bangladesh Test, with the hosts still finalizing their XI amid fitness 'niggles' in camp.
thread.changed: Play has now actually started: captain Pat Cummins won the toss and chose to bat first on a green, humid Darwin pitch, and Australia's confirmed XI includes both Cameron Green and Beau Webster, plus a returning Nathan Lyon, while Bangladesh has picked Ebadot Hossain and Mahmudul Hasan.

stories.title: Australia bat first as Bangladesh's 23-year wait for a Test tour Down Under finally ends in Darwin
stories.what_happened: Play began today in Darwin with Australia's captain **Pat Cummins** winning the toss and electing to bat first, fielding a full-strength side: Travis Head, Jake Weatherald, Marnus Labuschagne, Steven Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wicketkeeper), Beau Webster, Cummins, **Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood** — reuniting Australia's premier pace trio of Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood for the first time in this series. Bangladesh, led by captain **Najmul Hossain Shanto**, have signalled they may field two spinners even on a fast, bouncy Australian pitch, after being dismissed for just 54 in their warm-up match's second innings. Weather forecasts point to dry, sunny conditions for all five days.
key_points: Australia won the toss and chose to **bat first** in the opening Test at **Marrara Cricket Ground, Darwin** — Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
It's also Darwin's **first Test match in 22 years**, played in **clear, sunny conditions around 31°C**.
Australia's XI features their full frontline pace attack — **Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood together** — plus Travis Head, Steven Smith and captain Pat Cummins.
Bangladesh arrive under pressure after being **bowled out for just 54** in their second innings of the warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI.

depth.background: Bangladesh have toured Australia for Test cricket only rarely, and not at all in over two decades — a gap driven by scheduling, cricket-calendar priorities, and Australia's traditionally packed home summer. Darwin, in Australia's tropical Northern Territory, is an unusual and rarely-used Test venue, chosen partly to give Bangladesh conditions (heat, humidity) closer to what they're used to at home, even though the pitch and bounce still differ sharply from subcontinental cricket. Bangladesh's poor warm-up form has raised doubts about how competitive they can be against a full-strength Australian pace attack.

stories.title: Bangladesh still hasn't decided if its PM will visit India for the BRICS summit
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh's Foreign Minister **Khalilur Rahman** said the government is still **'currently reviewing'** Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's invitation for PM Tarique Rahman to attend the **18th BRICS Summit**, scheduled for **September 12-13 in New Delhi**. India confirmed on August 4 that it had extended the invite, with Rahman invited in his capacity as **BIMSTEC chairperson** rather than strictly as Bangladesh's head of government — a distinction Dhaka is weighing carefully. The foreign minister noted Rahman has multiple overseas commitments to juggle, including a planned trip to the **UN General Assembly** in New York, and that all engagements need to be considered together before a decision is made. This follows an earlier, still-unconfirmed invitation from Modi in February for a full bilateral visit with Rahman's family.
key_points: India confirmed on **August 4** it had invited Bangladesh PM **Tarique Rahman** to the **18th BRICS Summit** in New Delhi.
Bangladesh Foreign Minister **Khalilur Rahman** says the government is **'currently reviewing'** the invitation, with no decision yet.
The summit is scheduled for **September 12-13** in New Delhi; Rahman also has a UN General Assembly trip to weigh alongside it.
The invite came as **BIMSTEC chairperson**, not specifically as Bangladesh's PM — a nuance being parsed closely in Dhaka.
This is Modi's **second invitation** to Rahman this year, after a February invite for a bilateral visit went unanswered with a firm date.

depth.background: India-Bangladesh relations have been unsettled since **Sheikh Hasina's** government fell and she went into exile, with **Tarique Rahman** (leader of the BNP) now heading Bangladesh's government. Rahman notably chose Malaysia and China, not India, for his first official overseas trip after taking office — a signal read in Delhi as a deliberate distancing. Tensions were compounded further after Hasina gave a speech from Delhi that unsettled the relationship. **BRICS** is a bloc of major emerging economies (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and now expanded membership) that holds an annual summit; India is hosting this year's edition. Modi has now extended two separate invitations to Rahman in 2026 — one for a bilateral visit in February, and a follow-up for the BRICS summit — as India tries to keep a diplomatic door open despite the frosty start.

stories.title: Parliament curbs states' power to tax mining companies, in a win for the Centre over resource-rich states
stories.what_happened: The **Lok Sabha** passed the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 on **August 12**, and the **Rajya Sabha** cleared it the following day, **August 13**. The bill inserts a new **Section 9D**, under which states cannot impose taxes, cess, or other levies on mineral rights or mineral-bearing land based on the quantity or value of the mineral, or the royalty payable, except within conditions the Centre prescribes. The Centre will directly regulate major minerals — coal, limestone, iron ore, copper and manganese among them — while states retain authority over 49 minor minerals. The law also invalidates any state levies from before this amendment that companies haven't yet paid or that states haven't yet recovered, though money already collected will not have to be refunded. The bill becomes law once it receives the President's assent.
key_points: Parliament passed the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026**.
It bars states from taxing **mineral rights or mineral-bearing land** except on terms the Centre allows.
The Centre keeps control of major minerals like **coal, iron ore, copper and manganese**; states keep 49 minor minerals.
The law also **wipes out un-recovered past state levies**, though taxes already collected won't be refunded.
Mines Minister **G Kishan Reddy** says the goal is a **uniform mineral tax rate** nationwide, not less state revenue.

depth.background: This fight goes back to a landmark 2024 Supreme Court ruling that affirmed states' constitutional power to levy their own taxes on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land — on top of the royalty they already collect — and even allowed them to claim it retrospectively. Mineral-rich states like Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal moved to send large back-dated tax demands to mining companies, including state-run giants like Coal India, following that ruling. The Centre has now used ordinary legislation to substantially narrow what that Supreme Court ruling opened up.

stories.title: A Pakistan-linked militant front threatens Kashmiri Pandit government employees days before India's Independence Day
stories.what_happened: An outfit calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials say is a front for Lashkar-e-Taiba, posted an online letter listing the names and phone numbers of Kashmiri Pandit employees working under the Prime Minister's Special Employment Package. In response, the Jammu and Kashmir administration told roughly **2,800 employees** — Pandits, other migrants and those on the rehabilitation package — to stay away from their physical offices and work from home until **August 20**. Many of the named employees and their families have since left the Valley for Jammu, saying they intend to return only once the Independence Day period passes. Police have responded by stepping up night patrols, checkpoints and surveillance, including drones, at vulnerable locations and key entry and exit points across the region.
key_points: The **United Liberation Council**, a front for the Pakistan-based group Lashkar-e-Taiba, circulated an online letter naming Kashmiri Pandit employees along with their phone numbers
Around **2,800 Pandit, migrant and rehabilitation-package employees** have been told to work from home until **August 20**
Many affected families have fled to Jammu, planning to return only after the **August 15** celebrations
Police have added night patrols, checkpoints, frisking and drone surveillance across Srinagar and south Kashmir
The threat lands just before India's **80th Independence Day**, when security in the Valley is already at its tightest

depth.background: Kashmiri Pandits are Hindus native to the Kashmir Valley who were driven out by militant violence in a mass exodus in **1989-90**, during the early years of an insurgency against Indian rule. In recent years the government has run a rehabilitation package offering government jobs to encourage some Pandit families to return, part of a broader push to show that normal life has returned to Jammu and Kashmir since Delhi revoked the region's special autonomous status in **2019**. Lashkar-e-Taiba, the group blamed for the 2008 Mumbai attacks, has repeatedly targeted this return-and-resettlement push as a symbol of India's presence in the Valley it wants to disrupt.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of the Sri Lanka Tests as India hands uncapped Auqib Nabi a shock call-up
stories.what_happened: The BCCI announced a 15-member squad for the two-match Test series against Sri Lanka, naming Shubman Gill as captain and KL Rahul as vice-captain. Bumrah was left out entirely as he continues recovering from the knee injury sustained during India's ODI series in England, and uncapped fast bowler Auqib Nabi — who took 104 wickets in his last two Ranji Trophy seasons for Jammu and Kashmir, including 60 in this year's title-winning campaign — was named as his replacement. Gill, who had been under an injury cloud after hurting his finger in the warm-up match against a Sri Lanka Cricket XI, has since been passed fit to lead. Sai Sudharsan was separately ruled out of the series with a fractured toe. The first of the two Tests begins August 15 at Galle.
key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah** misses the two-match series as he continues recovering from a left-knee injury picked up in the England ODIs
**Shubman Gill** has been declared fit to captain the side after a finger scare in the warm-up match
**Auqib Nabi**, 26, earns his maiden India call-up after taking **104 wickets** across his last two Ranji Trophy seasons
KL Rahul is vice-captain; **Sai Sudharsan** is also out of the series with a fractured toe
The first Test starts **August 15** in Galle — India's first red-ball tour of Sri Lanka in **nine years**

depth.background: India last toured Sri Lanka for a Test series in 2017, when Virat Kohli's side completed a 3-0 clean sweep. This series is part of the 2025-27 World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, in which India currently sit fifth in the standings and Sri Lanka sixth. Bumrah, India's premier fast bowler, has been carefully managed through injuries in recent months, while allrounder Ravindra Jadeja's fitness has also been closely watched heading into this tour.

thread.previously: As of yesterday, Sai Sudharsan had been ruled out with a toe fracture and Shubman Gill's own participation was in doubt after a finger injury in the warm-up match.
thread.changed: Gill has now been passed fit and will captain the side, while Jasprit Bumrah has been confirmed out of the series entirely, with uncapped fast bowler Auqib Nabi drafted in as his replacement.

stories.title: FSSAI warns food influencers as data shows 98% of their ads now break advertising rules
stories.what_happened: FSSAI issued a public advisory this week cautioning food influencers and celebrities to carefully vet any brand claims before endorsing them, warning that promoting **unverified or misleading food claims** can lead to legal consequences for the endorser, not just the brand. The advisory came alongside fresh data from ASCI showing the ad-violation rate for influencer content has climbed sharply: **93% of ads were flagged as non-compliant or needing modification in 2021-22**, rising to **98% in 2025-26**. Over the same period, ASCI processed **37,532 total ad-violation cases**, of which **21.12% involved influencers**. FSSAI specifically called out common claims like 'boosts immunity' or 'rich in nutrients' as red flags when a brand can't substantiate them under existing food-safety and advertising rules. The advisory asks influencers to verify claims are truthful and compliant before lending their name and reach to a brand.
key_points: India's food regulator **FSSAI** warned influencers and celebrities against making unverified health or nutrition claims for food products.
The share of influencer food/health ads found non-compliant with rules jumped from **93% in 2021-22 to 98% in 2025-26**, per ASCI data.
**ASCI processed 37,532 ad-violation cases** in the period; over a fifth (**21.12%**) involved influencers specifically.
FSSAI singled out vague claims like 'boosts immunity' or 'rich in nutrients' when brands can't back them up with evidence.
Influencers who promote unverified claims can now face **legal consequences**, not just a warning.

depth.background: India's influencer-marketing industry has exploded over the past few years, and food and health brands are among the heaviest users of influencer endorsements to sell everything from supplements to snacks. The **Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI)**, a self-regulatory body, has been tracking ad-compliance rates for years, and **FSSAI** (the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) is the government regulator responsible for enforcing food-safety and labeling law. Regulators in India have increasingly focused on influencers specifically because their endorsements are seen as more trusted — and thus more persuasive, and more risky when false — than traditional ads.

stories.title: Delhi's H1N1 swine flu cases jump nearly sixfold this monsoon, with hospitals seeing a steady stream of patients
stories.what_happened: Delhi has logged **1,349 confirmed H1N1 cases** in 2026 so far, compared with just 229 over the same stretch last year — a nearly sixfold jump. Hospitals across the city, including major private facilities, report a steady stream of patients presenting with cough, cold, and high fever, with some outpatient departments seeing 7 to 10 H1N1 cases a day. Delhi's Health Minister Pankaj Singh said the government has ramped up testing across the city and set up dedicated wards and rooms in government hospitals to handle the rise. Doctors at AIIMS Delhi and elsewhere attribute the spike to the usual monsoon pattern of shifting temperatures, which favours the spread of influenza viruses.
key_points: Delhi has recorded **1,349 H1N1 cases** so far this year, versus just **229** in the same period of 2025 — almost a **sixfold rise**.
Hospitals report seeing around **7–10 H1N1 patients daily** in outpatient departments during the surge.
Delhi's Health Minister Pankaj Singh says **regular testing** is underway citywide and dedicated wards have been set up.
Doctors say **monsoon-season temperature swings** are a key driver of the seasonal rise in influenza cases.
The surge follows a broader pattern of **rising flu activity** across north India during the monsoon.

depth.background: H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a strain of seasonal influenza that tends to spike in India during the monsoon months as temperature and humidity swings help the virus spread more easily. Delhi's health system regularly tracks these seasonal infection numbers and adjusts hospital capacity accordingly.

stories.title: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament ends today, passing 11 bills after weeks of NEET-protest disruption
stories.what_happened: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan adjourned their respective Houses **sine die** on Thursday, officially closing the Monsoon Session. Despite the disruptions, both Houses together passed **11 bills** during the session, with the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill** clearing the Rajya Sabha by voice vote in the closing sitting. The Lok Sabha's final day opened with six stanzas of **Vande Mataram**, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi both present in the chamber. The Opposition's core demand — that Amit Shah personally address the Jantar Mantar police-crackdown allegations — was never formally resolved on the floor before the session closed.
key_points: Parliament's **Monsoon Session** was adjourned **sine die** today, closing on its originally scheduled date.
**11 bills** were passed across both Houses over the course of the session.
The **Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill** cleared the Rajya Sabha by **voice vote** in the final sitting.
The session opened on **July 20** and was repeatedly disrupted by protests over the **NEET-UG paper leak** police crackdown.

depth.background: "Sine die" adjournment means a legislative session ends completely with no date set to resume — different from a normal recess. stories.title: Tata Trusts formally kicks off the search for Chandrasekaran's successor, with Tata Steel's T V Narendran an early frontrunner

The committee will have **five members**: three jointly nominated by the two Tata Trusts, one from the Tata Sons board, and one independent outside member chosen by the board — with the two trusts also picking the committee's chair from among their three nominees. Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, can only step in as an *interim* Tata Sons chairman in exigent circumstances — not take the role permanently — under the same 2022 rules that created this succession puzzle in the first place.

**T V Narendran**, Tata Steel's global CEO and a 38-year Tata veteran, has emerged as an early frontrunner.
Other reported contenders include Tata Sons CFO **Saurabh Agrawal** and Tata Motors chief **Shailesh Chandra**.

stories.title: A US judge dismisses the criminal case against Gautam Adani — and Adani calls it 'humility, not vindication'
stories.what_happened: Judge Nicholas G. Garaufis of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York ruled on **Aug. 11** to dismiss, with prejudice, three criminal charges against Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani, and Adani Green Energy CEO Vneet Jaain — conspiracy to commit securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and securities fraud. The judge granted the dismissal at the DOJ's own request, but criticized the department for "irregularities," including bypassing its own investigators and what he described as colluding with defense counsel, and he refused to dismiss two related charges against **five other, non-Adani defendants** in the same case, saying prosecutors hadn't adequately justified that request. Court filings and the judge's own questioning probed whether Adani's November 2024 pledge to invest **$10 billion** in the United States played a role in the DOJ's decision to drop the case; a lawyer for Adani confirmed in a July filing that the group was "amenable" to following through on that pledge as part of resolving matters. Adani broke his silence on **Aug. 12** in a public address, saying the dismissal left him with "humility rather than a sense of vindication," and stating, "Trust is greater than any legal right." He drew a parallel to 2023, when — after the Hindenburg report triggered a stock rout — Adani Group was legally entitled to proceed with a ₹20,000 crore share sale but chose to cancel it and return investors' money instead.
key_points: Judge Nicholas Garaufis dismissed **three fraud and bribery charges** against Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani, and a top Adani Green executive, **with prejudice**.
The original indictment alleged a **$265 million bribery scheme** tied to solar power contracts in India.
The judge **sharply criticized** the DOJ for 'irregularities,' including bypassing its own investigators, even while granting the dismissal.
He specifically questioned whether Adani's pledge to invest **$10 billion in the US** influenced the DOJ's decision to drop the case.
Adani responded not with celebration but with a public statement: **'Trust is greater than any legal right.'**

depth.background: Gautam Adani is Asia's second-richest man and chairs the **Adani Group**, the Indian conglomerate that runs ports, power plants, airports, cement, and green-energy projects across the country. In November 2024, US prosecutors under the Biden administration indicted Adani and several executives, accusing them of paying over $250 million in bribes to Indian officials to win solar-power supply contracts, and of concealing this from US investors while raising capital there — allegations Adani has always denied. The case had shadowed Adani Group's stock price and its access to US capital markets for nearly two years, on top of a separate 2023 short-seller report by Hindenburg Research that briefly wiped tens of billions off the group's market value.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs past 265 as more than 2,700 remain reported missing
stories.what_happened: As of Wednesday, Colombian authorities had confirmed at least **265 dead**, a sharp rise from the 220-227 figures reported the previous day, with officials warning the number will likely keep climbing as rescuers reach areas still cut off by blocked roads. Separately, volunteer-run tracking databases — which count family reports the government hasn't yet verified — put the number of people still unaccounted for at **more than 2,700**. Rescue crews have logged over **70 aftershocks** since the initial quake and are using thermal-imaging drones, cadaver dogs and specialized rubble-clearing equipment to keep searching in Cali, where a woman was pulled alive from debris almost 30 hours after the quake and a baby was rescued from a collapsed apartment building. The material toll is also severe: more than **1,100 homes destroyed** and **8,300 more damaged** across the affected region. Colombia had initially asked for help from only the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel, but has since widened its request, with Peru now confirming it will send volunteer rescuers too.
key_points: The confirmed death toll from Monday's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has climbed past **265**, up from the 220-227 range reported a day earlier.
Volunteer networks tracking family reports say more than **2,700 people are still unaccounted for**, far above the government's own missing-persons count.
Rescue teams have recorded more than **70 aftershocks** and are using **thermal-imaging drones and cadaver dogs** to search collapsed buildings in Cali.
More than **1,100 homes have been destroyed** and **8,300 damaged**, with roads into the epicenter near San José del Palmar still blocked.
Dramatic rescues continue even past the 72-hour survival window — including a **baby pulled alive from a collapsed Cali apartment block**.

depth.background: A **7.4-magnitude earthquake** struck Colombia's Pacific coast on Monday, the strongest the country has recorded in a decade. It hit hardest in the western Chocó region, near the town of San José del Palmar, and shook the capital Bogotá and the city of Cali. The disaster is the **first major crisis test** for Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, whose government initially limited international rescue offers to just four countries — a decision now under public criticism as the scale of the damage has become clearer.

thread.changed: The confirmed toll has now climbed past 265, volunteer networks report more than 2,700 people still unaccounted for, and rescuers using thermal drones and dog teams have kept pulling survivors — including a baby — from the rubble in Cali even after the survival window closed.

stories.title: Supreme Court signals it will send the Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Idgah 'who represents Hindus' dispute back to the Allahabad High Court
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court was hearing an appeal from plaintiffs in the original 2020 suit (suit no. 1, which seeks removal of the mosque), who challenged an **Allahabad High Court ruling** that let a different, later group of petitioners (suit no. 17) be treated as the representative voice for 'all devotees of Lord Krishna' in the case. The bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva observed that the High Court had made this designation **without issuing notice to the plaintiffs in the other suits**, meaning those parties never got a chance to argue against it. The judges indicated they are inclined to send the representation question back down to the Allahabad High Court so it can be reheard properly, with all plaintiffs given notice and an opportunity to be heard this time. The Court granted an adjournment until **September 2**, when it is expected to formalise this order.
key_points: The Supreme Court said it is **inclined to remand** a key procedural fight in the long-running Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Idgah case back to the **Allahabad High Court**.
The dispute is over **which plaintiffs get to represent** 'all devotees of Lord Krishna' in the underlying suit — not the core temple-mosque dispute itself.
The High Court had let one Hindu party (suit no. 17) represent all devotees **without formally notifying** the plaintiffs from other, earlier suits, including suit no. 1.
A bench of **Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva** wants all plaintiffs given a fair hearing on the representation question before the case moves forward.
The matter has been adjourned to **September 2** for a formal order.

depth.background: The Krishna Janmabhoomi-Shahi Idgah dispute is one of India's most sensitive ongoing religious-property cases, centred on a mosque in Mathura that Hindu petitioners say sits on the site of Lord Krishna's birthplace, and which some groups want removed or partially reclaimed. It sits alongside the Ayodhya Ram Mandir dispute as one of a handful of major Hindu-Muslim religious site disputes working through India's courts over the past decade, and both sides have long anticipated it could become similarly high-profile. Multiple separate lawsuits by different Hindu petitioner groups have been filed over the years, each claiming to represent devotees' interests — which is what created today's narrower procedural fight over who actually gets to be the 'lead' plaintiff group in court.

stories.title: Spain just had its first total solar eclipse since 1905 — and it's only the opener in an unheard-of three-eclipse run through 2028
stories.what_happened: On Wednesday, the Moon's shadow swept from **Greenland and Iceland across northern Spain** as the Sun set, delivering totality — the brief window when the Moon fully blocks the Sun — to an estimated **15 million people**, most of them in Spain. It was the **first total solar eclipse over mainland Europe since 1999** and mainland Spain's first since **1905**. Scientists used the rare darkness to study the Sun's **corona**, the outer atmosphere normally invisible in daylight, which affects space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids. What makes this moment bigger than a single afternoon is the calendar that follows: Spain will see a second total eclipse on **August 2, 2027**, then an annular eclipse on **January 26, 2028** — a three-eclipse sequence astronomers are calling the 'Iberian trio', the first cluster of total eclipses over mainland Europe this century.
key_points: Monday's eclipse was Spain's first total solar eclipse in mainland territory since **1905** — 121 years.
A second total eclipse will cross Spain again on **August 2, 2027**, visible from the Iberian Peninsula down into North Africa and the Middle East.
A third eclipse — an **annular** ('ring of fire') eclipse where the Moon doesn't fully cover the Sun — follows on **January 26, 2028**.
Astronomers are calling it the **'Iberian trio'**, an occurrence so rare that few countries have experienced three eclipses this close together.
The totality path this week reached as far as **Palma, Valencia, Zaragoza, Bilbao and León**, with observers getting up to 1 minute 50 seconds of darkness.

depth.background: Total solar eclipses happen somewhere on Earth every year or two, but any single spot on the planet typically waits **centuries** between them, because the Moon's shadow is only about 100 miles wide and sweeps across a thin, fast-moving path. Mainland Spain's last one was in **1905**; mainland Europe as a whole hadn't seen one since **1999**. That's what made this week's event, and the discovery that two more are coming within two years, so unusual to scientists who track these cycles.

thread.previously: We covered Tuesday's eclipse as it happened: totality began around 15:34 GMT and swept from Iceland to Spain, lasting up to 2 minutes 18 seconds, watched by an estimated 15 million people, and coinciding with the Perseid meteor shower.
thread.changed: Now that the event has passed, the bigger story is emerging: this wasn't a one-off. It's the first of **three consecutive total or annular solar eclipses to cross Spain by 2028** — a concentration of eclipses astronomers say almost no country has ever seen in such a short span, turning Spain into a hub for eclipse tourism for the rest of the decade.

stories.title: India's retail inflation hits a 19-month high of 4.45% in July, driven by pricier food
stories.what_happened: The National Statistics Office reported that India's retail inflation rose to 4.45% in July, its highest level in 19 months and up from 4.38% in June. The increase was mainly driven by food prices, where inflation rose to 5.52% from 5.32% the month before. This marks the second consecutive month inflation has printed above the RBI's 4% target, following sixteen straight months where it had stayed below that level. The RBI's own projections, released alongside its August rate decision, anticipate inflation will keep climbing in the near term and peak around 5.9% in the October-December quarter of this fiscal year, before easing again.
key_points: **Consumer price index (CPI) inflation** rose to **4.45% in July**, up from 4.38% in June — the **highest reading in 19 months**.
**Food inflation** was the main driver, climbing to **5.52%** from 5.32% the previous month.
This is the **second straight month** that inflation has stayed above the **RBI's 4% target**, after 16 months of running below it.
The RBI itself expects headline inflation to keep rising and **peak near 5.9% in the October-December quarter**.
Data was released by the **National Statistics Office (NSO)** on August 12.

depth.background: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures how much prices for a broad basket of everyday goods and services — like food, fuel and housing — have changed for typical households, and it's India's main gauge of retail inflation. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) targets keeping CPI inflation around 4%, using it as the main input for interest-rate decisions. Just a week earlier, the RBI's rate-setting committee had held its key policy rate steady at 5.25% for a fourth straight meeting, citing a wish for 'greater clarity' on where inflation was heading before acting either way.

stories.title: A total solar eclipse sweeps across mainland Europe for the first time since 1999
stories.what_happened: Totality began around **15:34 GMT** and swept west to east across the path, lasting up to two minutes eighteen seconds at its longest point. An estimated **15 million people**, most of them in Spain, were positioned inside the path of totality, with Iceland catching the eclipse in the late afternoon before the Moon's shadow raced on toward Spain near sunset. The event doubled as a triple sky show: it coincided with the peak of the **Perseid meteor shower** and followed a rare six-planet alignment visible before dawn the same day. Scientists in Spain and Iceland used the brief window of darkness to study the Sun's corona, a layer of the Sun's atmosphere that is normally washed out by direct sunlight and can only be observed properly during totality or with specialized instruments.
key_points: The Moon fully blocked the Sun over **Iceland, Greenland and northern Spain** — the first total eclipse seen from mainland Europe in **27 years**.
Up to **15 million people**, mostly in Spain, sat inside the narrow 'path of totality' where the sky went dark in daytime.
Totality lasted up to **2 minutes 18 seconds** at its longest point along the path.
The eclipse coincided with the peak of the **Perseid meteor shower** and a rare pre-dawn alignment of six planets.
Scientists used the brief darkness to study the Sun's **corona**, its outer atmosphere that's normally invisible in daylight.

depth.background: A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, and its shadow is small enough that only a narrow strip of the planet — the 'path of totality' — experiences full darkness. Because the Moon's shadow is only about 100-160 km wide, most eclipses cross oceans or sparsely populated land; this is the **first one to sweep across mainland Europe since 1999**, and the first ever recorded from the Iberian Peninsula in over a century. The path today ran from Siberian Russia through Greenland and Iceland before reaching northern Spain and Portugal just before sunset.

stories.title: Tata stocks drag Sensex lower as investors digest Chandrasekaran's shock resignation, oil pressure adds to the drop

stories.title: India says it is 'examining' Bangladesh's renewed request to extradite Sheikh Hasina
stories.what_happened: India's government said it is **'examining' Bangladesh's request for the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina** in line with established legal processes, responding a day after Bangladesh's interim leadership renewed its extradition demand during a meeting between India's High Commissioner, Dinesh Trivedi, and Bangladesh's Prime Minister, Tarique Rahman. Hasina, 78, was convicted by Bangladesh's special International Crimes Tribunal on charges of crimes against humanity related to the deadly 2024 protest crackdown and sentenced to death in November. India's statement stops short of any commitment on timing or outcome, keeping the request under review rather than acting on it.
key_points: India says it is **'examining'** Bangladesh's latest formal request to extradite **Sheikh Hasina** through established legal channels.
This is the **third official extradition request** Dhaka has sent since Hasina fled to India in August 2024.
Hasina, now 78, was **convicted and sentenced to death** in November by a special tribunal in Dhaka for crimes against humanity tied to the 2024 protest crackdown.
The statement came a day after **India's High Commissioner met Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman**, where Dhaka renewed its demand.
India has **not committed to a timeline or decision** — 'examining' signals the request is being processed, not approved.

depth.background: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's longtime prime minister, fled to India in August 2024 after a student-led uprising forced the collapse of her government amid a violent crackdown on protesters. Bangladesh's interim and subsequent governments have since pursued Hasina through Dhaka's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT), and in November she was convicted in absentia of **crimes against humanity** and sentenced to death over her government's response to the 2024 protests. India and Bangladesh have a bilateral extradition treaty, but India has so far neither granted nor formally rejected Dhaka's earlier requests, leaving Hasina's status in India in diplomatic limbo for close to two years.
